title: LG Energy Solution to supply 46,100 round cells to Mercedes - electrive.com
content:
According to a media report, LG Energy Solution will supply round cells with a diameter of 46 millimeters and a height of 100 millimeters - a novel format - for Mercedes-Benz's next-gen EVs. Deliveries are set to begin in 2028.
Image: LG Energy Solution
This is according to a report by the usually well-informed South Korean portal
The Elec
, which specifies that the 46100 round cells are a new cylindrical battery cell format in the 46-series that LG Energy Solution has not yet unveiled. According to the portal, the company is expected to begin setting up production lines next year and start delivering the batteries from 2028.
The Elec
cites industry insiders for this news and notes that there are plans to establish a first production line for 46100 battery cells at LG Energy Solution’s Polish plant in Wrocław – with Mercedes-Benz as the customer. Additionally, LGES is reportedly considering investments in module assembly, where the cells will be combined into modules. However, this information has not been officially confirmed.
For context: the 46-series battery cells, particularly the 4680 round cells (with a height of 80 mm), are primarily used by several automakers – most notably Tesla. Formats such as 4695 and 46120 (with heights of 95 mm and 120 mm, respectively) are also available but less common. However, LGES is one of the suppliers with a broad portfolio of 46-series cells. At the end of last year, the South Korean company began producing 4695 cells at its Ochang plant, and by the end of this year,
earlier reports indicated
that production of “diverse 46-Series cylindrical cells, ranging from 4680 to 46120 cells” would start at the US plant in Arizona. However, it was previously unknown that LGES was also preparing a version with a height of 100 millimetres.
The Elec
also reports that LG Energy Solution is preparing a facility for the new 46100 cell type in Ochang to adapt it to the specifications of the planned mass-production line in Poland. It comes as little surprise that Mercedes-Benz is set to become the main customer. Since October 2024, the two companies have already signed four long-term supply agreements. However, the partnership is not exclusive: in April, the Stuttgart-based automaker also signed its first long-term supply contract for electric vehicle batteries
with Samsung SDI
. Additionally, CATL is part of the supplier network. Previously, the company had also sourced battery cells from SK On and Farasis.

title: Exide Industries commissions 6GWh first phase of India Li cells plant – Batteries International
content: Exide Energy Solutions (EESL) has announced the commissioning of the 6GWh first phase of its lithium ion cell manufacturing facility in India. EESL, a subsidiary of Exide Industries, said the Karnataka state facility achieved the milestone on September 23. The achievement came more than four years after lead battery major Exide announced it was also venturing into the lithium sector with Chinese support. Exide confirmed in March 2022 it had agreed a long-term technical collaboration deal with China’s SVOLT Energy Technology for lithium ion cell manufacturing. As part of that deal, SVOLT granted Exide an irrevocable right and licence to use, exploit and commercialise technology and know-how owned by them for the venture. Batteries International reported previously that the first phase of the facility was originally planned to be operational by the end of 2024. In December 2025, Pravin Ramchandra Saraf took over as MD and CEO of EESL following the resignation of Mandar Deo. title: China pushes multi-chemistry innovation in ‘first dedicated national battery plan’ – Batteries International
content: China has unveiled a blueprint to develop its ‘new-type battery sector’, targeting industry growth and an expansion of innovation capabilities across the entire industrial chain by 2030. The blueprint defines new-type batteries as high-efficiency devices or systems for storing and converting electrical energy, including lithium, sodium and flow batteries, state news agency Xinhua announced on September 28. Nan Cewen, a professor at Tsinghua University and an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said the ambitious programme for batteries was the country’s first dedicated national-level plan for the battery industry. Nan said measures include accelerating technological breakthroughs needed for industrial-scale production of all-solid-state batteries and developing a product supply system centred on lithium batteries, complemented by sodium and flow batteries. The blueprint, released under China’s 15th five-year plan for 2026-2030, envisions the initial large-scale application of all-solid-state batteries and a cycle life of 15,000 cycles for long-life lithium batteries by 2030. China also aims to achieve breakthroughs in advanced electrode materials, new electrolytes and high-end auxiliary materials, in addition to making “major progress in the development of new battery systems”, according to the government. EVs and humanoid robotics are among applications fuelling demand for high-performance batteries in China — while battery-based energy storage is being used to support renewable energy integration and improve power grid stability, the government said. Xinhua said official data showed China’s new-type battery industry saw its output value exceed Rmb1 trillion ($149 billion) during the 14th five-year plan for 2021-2025. Work will also focus on improving the safety and ‘all-climate performance’ of batteries for new energy vehicles, strengthening intellectual property protection and improving battery life-cycle traceability. A leading industry executive said in an article for Batteries International earlier this year that, for Western nations to compete with China, the focus must be on discovering breakthrough chemistries and accelerating the progression from lab to volume production. title: UK issues Tesla Powerwall 2 ESS fire risk alert – Batteries International
content:
Energy Storage, Lithium, News
Read Later
Tesla discontinued Powerwall 2 in 2025 in favour of Powerwall 3 (pictured)
The UK’s Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS) has warned of a potential fire risk from Tesla Powerwall 2 ESS systems, triggering a replacement programme for affected units.
The OPSS issued the warning on September 28, saying affected US-origin Powerwall 2 models, designed largely for residential energy storage, presented a fire risk because certain battery cells might develop internal defects over time.
An investigation identified that battery cells manufactured by a third party may contain excessive lithium plating, which can lead to cracking of the cell casing, OPSS said.
“This may result in an internal short circuit and subsequent thermal runaway, increasing the risk of the battery overheating and catching fire.”
The product does not meet the requirements of UK electrical equipment safety regulations, OPSS said.
Tesla has remotely discharged an unspecified number of most affected Powerwall 2 units pending replacement, while any remaining affected units are being discharged by Tesla technicians.
OPSS said Tesla advised customers to ensure their Powerwall 2 units remain online and to check the Tesla app for a notification confirming whether their units are affected. If a replacement is required, customers should contact their original Tesla certified installer to arrange installation.
Tesla’s Powerwall 2 replacement programme web site says the company is disabling and replacing units that have faulted in operation and are no longer meeting Tesla standards. These units will be replaced free of charge.
Discharged units do not pose an operational risk, the company said.
Meanwhile, Tesla has yet to respond to questions from
Batteries International
about the number of Powerwall 2 systems that are affected in the UK — and whether a worldwide Powerwall 2 replacement programme has been launched.
Tesla discontinued Powerwall 2 in 2025 and shifted focus to Powerwall 3. Powerwall 2 was marketed as a fully-integrated AC battery system for residential or light commercial use with rechargeable lithium ion battery packs providing energy storage for solar self-consumption, time-based control and backup.

title: Clarios partners Romania’s Piaxo to expand Na ion R&D – Batteries International
content:
News, Other Chemistries
Read Later
Federico Morales-Zimmermann, Clarios VP & GM (left) with Piaxo CEO Ion Petic
Clarios is further expanding its R&D presence in Europe as part of a new sodium ion battery partnership in Romania with automotive engineering company Piaxo.
The partnership was announced on September 30, just a few weeks after the US-based battery giant
stepped up
its Na ion battery tech partnership with Sweden’s Altris to start pilot-scale and small-series production in Slovakia.
Cooperation with Piaxo will centre on the Romanian firm’s high-tech engineering complex and test lab in Timișoara, although both companies will maintain their separate organisations and have distinct roles and responsibilities.
The Timișoara centre supports R&D projects in areas such as battery management systems for next-generation energy storage systems including Na ion and lithium ion batteries, as well as inverter and supercapacitor technologies essential for modern vehicles and safety-critical applications.
Clarios said Piaxo continues to expand its engineering organisation at the centre and now employs nearly 50 engineers.
Ion Petic, Piaxo’s CEO, said the partnership creates opportunities for his company’s engineers to contribute to globally relevant engineering work, build specialised expertise and collaborate with international engineering teams on increasingly complex technology programmes.
Batteries International
reported earlier this year that Clarios, which owns the VARTA Automotive brand, continues to invest in its mainstay lead acid business.
In August, the company
confirmed
a major deal to source low-carbon lead for its battery manufacturing plants in Europe, the Middle East and Africa from Swedish mining and metals company Boliden.

title: Future of Nyrstar’s Budel smelter under review amid soaring energy costs, global turmoil – Batteries International
content: The future of Nyrstar’s Budel zinc smelter in the Netherlands is uncertain after the group launched a review against a backdrop of soaring energy costs and geopolitical instability. Trafigura-owned Nyrstar said on September 24 the review will consider future options for the site which produces zinc and zinc alloys, sulfuric acid and ‘Budel Leach Product’ — containing lead and precious metals used as a raw material by secondary smelters. Nyrstar’s announcement came just a month after it completed a 71-day major shutdown and maintenance programme at Budel. Key tasks included the installation of new absorption towers for sulfuric acid and works on the sulfuric acid plant. However, the global multi-metals business said its review was needed following the Dutch government’s national budget for 2027, unveiled on September 15. Nyrstar said the government’s decision not to include provisions for grid cost mitigation for energy-intensive industries in the budget would put Budel under further pressure. The Budel review is set to ramp up uncertainty on the global sulfuric acid market, as exclusively reported by Batteries International last April. Nevertheless, Nyrstar said the plant’s competitive position has come under increasing pressure over recent years amid extremely challenging conditions for zinc smelters globally. Chinese overcapacity, intense competition for feedstock, historically low treatment and refining charges, and elevated European energy costs are placing the entire Western smelting industry under severe pressure, the group said. These challenges are compounded by high total energy costs in the Netherlands and differences in competitive conditions compared with neighbouring countries. The group said that while it recognised steps taken to address the competitiveness of energy-intensive industry in the Netherlands, its assessment was that the overall budget framework did not sufficiently address the structural total energy-cost disadvantage faced by Budel compared with neighbouring European markets. CEO Guido Janssen said Budel’s operations would continue as normal while the review is underway, but warned operations continued to face significant pressure in terms of tough market conditions, elevated energy prices and historically low treatment and refining charges over a sustained period. “The operation is losing money every year and the conditions for next year look particularly difficult, given rising energy costs, together with a lack of supportive government policy,” he said. “This is a significant decision point for Budel. The review will allow us to carefully assess the site’s position and the options available, while continuing to consider whether concrete action can materially improve the business case.” Budel, founded in 1892, is in the southeast of the Netherlands, close to its customers in the country and major industrial centres in Belgium, Germany, Luxembourg and northern France. Nyrstar did not disclose the latest production figures for Budel. However, analysis published by DKL Engineering’s Acid Plant Database recently said the site produces more than 320,000 tonnes of high-quality sulfuric acid annually, together with around 81,000 wet tonnes of Budel Leach Product. title: Data centre investments help drive Q2 ESS record in US – Batteries International
content: The US energy storage market installed a record 19GWh in the second quarter of this year — a 17% rise over the same period in 2025 — buoyed by hyper investment activity in the data centre market, latest analysis shows. Utility-scale ESS deployments totalled 4.7GW/17.6GWh during the period, down 8% year-on-year in megawatt terms as key markets are saturating, according to the quarterly US Energy Storage Monitor (ESM), released on September 22 by Wood Mackenzie Power & Renewables and the American Clean Power Association. Data centre buildout boosted the US storage outlook across all segments, because storage can provide capacity faster, cheaper and more reliably than gas alone, ESM said. As hyperscalers increasingly face grid-connection bottlenecks, utility-scale storage will enable speed to power for data centres, either on-site to manage asset load or at the system level to support evolving grid needs. “Distributed storage’s value proposition is broadening beyond customer centric benefits to include grid services, as the industry seeks to position virtual power plants (VPPs) as a key enabler of load growth,” said ESM. A separate report — Wood Mackenzie’s Q3 2026 Power & Renewables Compass — published on October 1, said the race to build data centre projects has made ‘speed to power’ a top priority. David Brown, Wood Mackenzie’s director of global integrated energy research, said: “New high-voltage transmission is the traditional answer, but decade-long build times are far too slow.” The report considers three ‘faster infrastructure pathways’: VPPs, deliverable in 6-18 months, with data centre buyers pursuing a 19GW pipeline led by the US market, but where new utility and ISO regulations are needed to scale VPPs further; Grid enhancing technologies — unlocking 5%-50% more capacity from existing transmission in weeks to 18 months; Around-the-meter projects — bypassing the grid entirely, these projects with equipment secured and voltage ride-through compliance confirmed “can be delivered in 24-48 months”, but in-flight and early-stage projects could face three to six-year equipment wait times. The latest reports are in line with a forecast made last May by Goldman Sachs Commodities Research where US data centre power demand is predicted to more than double to 66GW in 2027 from 31GW in 2025, driven by an accelerating buildout of AI infrastructure. However, Goldman Sachs warned that only about 50%-60% of data centre capacity scheduled for the next one to two years was expected to come online on time amid delays and cancellations. Batteries International reported this August that Energy Vault had agreed a deal to supply battery storage, grid-forming power conversion systems and AI infrastructure control software for a 1.25GW hyperscale datacentre project in Texas. The company said it would work with an undisclosed partner to jointly develop the integrated, off-grid power systems in a deal worth around $500 million-$600 million. title: Sunlight USA launches online ‘battery match’ guide for industry – Batteries International
content: Sunlight Batteries USA has launched a digital selector guide to match the firm’s lead acid batteries to a range of forklifts and other equipment used in warehouses and distribution centres. The American arm of the Greece-based Sunlight Group announced the launch of the online service on September 30 — aimed at providing a faster, more efficient starting point to identify a compatible lead acid battery based on truck and application requirements. Sunlight said the move comes at a time when US manufacturing is navigating increasingly varied equipment needs, greater automation and demand spikes that no longer follow a predictable peak season. When a battery must be replaced or new equipment is added to a fleet, customers may already know the truck and battery type they need — but they still need to identify the corresponding product and part number in a supplier’s portfolio. Sunlight said its guide covers forklift specifications, battery dimensions, connectivity requirements and operating conditions, helping users narrow the available options by forklift manufacturer, model, voltage and technology. The simplified digital system matches users’ specifications with a compatible Sunlight lead acid battery, including its material number, dimensions, weight, amp-hour capacity, and kilowatt-hour rating. The lead and lithium manufacturer said later iterations of the guide are planned for lithium batteries using LFP and NMC chemistries, as well as chargers. Chris Scott, CEO of Sunlight’s US arm, said: “Our customers are focused on keeping their equipment and operations moving. Finding the right battery to keep their business moving should not add unnecessary complexity to their day.” The post Sunlight USA launches online ‘battery match’ guide for industry appeared first on Batteries International .

title: Stryten pledges battery investments boost as C&D Trojan acquisition finalised – Batteries International
content: Stryten Energy has formally completed its acquisition of C&D Technologies and Trojan Battery — marking one of the largest consolidations in the North American lead battery sector in recent years. Stryten announced the completion on October 1, more than two months after revealing the deal to establish a powerhouse manufacturing base for transportation, industrial, critical infrastructure and military applications. Financial terms of the acquisition have not been disclosed, but a raft of investments are now planned, including in AGM battery manufacture and products as well as services for sectors including defence and telecoms. The combined company operates 18 battery manufacturing and component facilities across the US, Mexico and China, with a global workforce of around 4,800. Stryten said the company will continue to operate under the Stryten Energy name while preserving the C&D Technologies and Trojan Battery product brands. The company will expand investments in US battery manufacturing capacity, facility modernisation, equipment upgrades and workforce development. In addition, there are plans to expand the firm’s AGM battery manufacturing capacity to meet growing demand from automotive aftermarket customers for start-stop and hybrid vehicle applications requiring high-performance batteries. Mike Judd, Stryten president and CEO, said the move brings together decades of manufacturing expertise, innovation and customer commitment under one company. “We intend to accelerate investments in domestic battery manufacturing capacity, advanced energy storage technologies and military production capabilities, creating a stronger company with the scale, technology portfolio and manufacturing capabilities to support growing customer demand across transportation, speciality motive, data centre, telecommunications, industrial and military applications.” Judd said the addition of C&D Trojan expands the firm’s ability to serve the automotive aftermarket with advanced AGM battery technology. The combination of the companies’ military battery portfolios creates one of the most comprehensive domestic battery platforms supporting US defence, government and national security applications, Judd said. Planned investments will support the scaling of US-based manufacturing capacity to meet increasing demand for batteries used in land warfare systems, air defence systems, naval surface/undersea systems, logistics, reserve power systems, nuclear power and other essential infrastructure. title: New probe as fire-damaged California BESS hit by another blaze – Batteries International
content: Firefighters have tackled another fire at Vistra’s Moss Landing lithium ion BESS in California — a facility still undergoing a clean-up after a devastating blaze in January 2025. The California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE) confirmed it was called to the site again last month, after a fire broke out in the morning of September 18 and was eventually contained one day later. The cause of the original and latest fires are still unknown. In this September’s incident, which is under investigation, CAL FIRE said crews arrived to find smoke and fire coming from the north side of the facility. Firefighters also conducted evacuations and accounted for plant personnel while working to stabilise the situation. The official Moss Landing response web site set up by Vistra to publicise developments since January 2025 did not comment on the latest fire. However, campaign group ‘Never Again Moss Landing’ claimed the latest fire came just two weeks after the US Environmental Protection Agency and Vistra had started the final phase of clean-up. The group claimed local residents were advised to shelter in their homes as emergency crews tackled the fire. Batteries International reported in April 2026 that part of Moss Landing would never return to service. Vistra said then that ‘Moss 100’, one of three BESS systems at the site, would not return to service because the cost of recommissioning would outweigh potential future revenues. Meanwhile, Vistra said it was continuing to evaluate the potential restart of another part of the 300MW facility ― and revealed the cause of the 2025 was still unknown. University of Michigan partnership to train next generation of battery engineers, support North American manufacturing.
Toyota Motor North America officially opened its Toyota Battery Center of North America (TBC) on October 1, marking an expansion of the automaker's battery development capabilities and its commitment to electrification in the region. The 30,000-square-foot, $50 million facility is located at Toyota's existing R&D headquarters in York Township near Saline, less than an hour’s drive from Detroit (and a 20-minute drive from this writer’s office in Ann Arbor). The center will serve as a central hub for battery evaluation and development across the full lifecycle—from raw material sourcing to customer applications and recycling.
Strategic investment amid market transition
The facility opening comes as the US EV market navigates a complicated transition period. As we’ve reported, though EV sales continue to grow in absolute numbers, adoption rates have fallen short of earlier industry projections, with consumers citing concerns about vehicle cost, charging infrastructure availability, and range anxiety.
Related:
Battery Breaking-News Headlines
At the same time, Chinese manufacturers have emerged as formidable competitors in EV and battery technology, leveraging significant government support, integrated supply chains, and aggressive pricing strategies. This competitive pressure has intensified calls for domestic investment in battery R&D and manufacturing capabilities.
In response to these market dynamics, automakers have recalibrated their electrification strategies. Some have delayed all-electric model launches or scaled back production targets, while others have renewed focus on hybrid technologies as a bridge solution. Toyota's approach—maintaining what it calls a "multi-pathway strategy"—positions the company to serve diverse customer needs across the electrification spectrum.
The new Michigan facility directly supports this strategy by enabling development and testing across multiple powertrain technologies simultaneously. This flexibility may prove advantageous as market preferences continue to evolve and as different regions adopt electrification at varying paces.
The investment also aligns with broader industry efforts to localize battery development and manufacturing in North America, reducing dependence on overseas supply chains and positioning domestic facilities to respond more quickly to regional market demands and regulatory requirements.
While the Michigan facility represents a significant commitment to R&D, Toyota's largest battery investment remains in North Carolina, where the company has invested nearly $14 billion in a battery production facility with plans for more than 5,000 jobs.
Related:
Editors' Roundtable: Significant Battery News in September 2026
Toyota's battery plant in Liberty, NC. Credit: Toyota
Comprehensive testing capabilities
Engineers and technicians at the facility will assess battery performance and develop technologies for hybrid, plug-in hybrid, hydrogen, and fully electric vehicles. The center will support Toyota's North American manufacturing network, including battery manufacturing operations in North Carolina and vehicle assembly plants across the continent.
"Toyota has long been at the forefront of battery development," stated Keita Moritsu, Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer at Toyota Motor North America R&D. "This center is where that leadership expands to North America — and where we're building its next chapter."
Jordan Choby, Group Vice President of Powertrain, emphasized the customer benefits of having advanced testing capabilities closer to North American operations. "For Toyota customers, this facility means Toyota engineers can detect and resolve field concerns faster and closer to the source," Choby stated. "It also means we can develop longer-lasting batteries designed to perform in the conditions American drivers face every day."
an interview with WXYZ
, Choby added: "We're now the bridge between some of the most advanced battery development teams and our North American manufacturing."

Sodium-Ion Battery Production Scales Up as CBAK and HiTHIUM Target 2027 Commercial Deployment
Strategic location and political support
Toyota first announced plans for the battery center in 2023. The company's decision to locate the facility in Michigan reflects the state's automotive ecosystem advantages, including supplier networks and university partnerships.
The center represents the latest milestone in Toyota's more than 50-year history in Michigan, where the company now employs 2,000 people on its York Township campus,
according to WEMU
Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer attended the grand opening ceremony and praised the investment as strengthening the state's leadership in advanced automotive manufacturing. "We are proud to welcome this investment by Toyota that positions Michigan as the best place to build the future," Whitmer stated.
Congresswoman Debbie Dingell (D-MI 6) emphasized the facility's role in maintaining American competitiveness against foreign rivals. Investments like this one from Toyota will help keep out Chinese influence in electric vehicle technology, Dingell said, according to WEMU.
The battery center "is a tangible representation of what it means to keep Michigan at the cutting edge of innovation," Dingell said. "This facility is creating good-paying high-tech jobs, supporting American manufacturing, and ensuring that the next generation of automotive innovation happens right here in Michigan."
Academic partnership and workforce development
Toyota will provide research access to the University of Michigan Electric Vehicle Center, allowing students and research partners to benefit from the facility's testing and evaluation capabilities. As a founding member of the Electric Vehicle Center, this collaboration is part of Toyota's commitment to developing the next generation of battery engineers and technicians in Michigan.
"Researchers and students will work alongside industry experts to research cutting-edge technology, and this partnership will prepare students to tackle the biggest challenges of the future, right here at home," Whitmer said, according to WEMU.
The Michigan battery center will support evaluation of batteries produced at the North Carolina facility as well as Toyota's vehicle manufacturing plants across North America.

title: Future of Battery Manufacturing: Risks and Opportunities
content:
Battery Manufacturing
Batteries
Industry Outlook
Market Analysis
Interviews
Keynote at The Battery Show North America highlights the 'Technological Iron Curtain' reshaping global battery manufacturing dynamics.
October 2, 2026
3 Min Read
Reshoring and the reindustrialization of the US represent significant pent-up demand for batteries.
Courtesy of Narvikk / iStock / Getty Images Plus
While the risks and opportunities for the battery space echo the challenges of other industries, opportunities and demand are likely to be anything but common — and in fact will likely be exceptional.
Risks and opportunities in battery manufacturing
That’s the perspective of Jason Schenker, president of Prestige Economics, chairman of The Futurist Institute, and keynote speaker at Informa’s
Battery Show North America
in Detroit from Oct. 12-15.
Schenker’s presentation, “The Future of Battery Manufacturing: Risks and Opportunities in the Age of AI and Cold War Two,” will spotlight how US economic mobilization for a wartime-ready economy is supporting
domestic battery manufacturing
. “At the same time, AI power needs are also supporting domestic manufacturing, industrial investment and power infrastructure buildouts that are both on-grid and behind the meter,” Schenker asserted.
The challenges facing this new paradigm of manufacturing are all too familiar, he added: a tight labor force and high labor costs, supply chain disruption risks, and Cold War Two geopolitical challenges. That said, “rising power demand, industrial-scale power storage needs and high petroleum fuel prices are all likely to support battery demand.”
Related:
Jennifer Granholm: Battery Company’s Move Is ‘A Wake-Up Call for American Manufacturing’
Jason Schenker, President of Prestige Economics, chairman of The Futurist Institute. Courtesy of Jason Schenker.
The role of industrial-scale batteries in energy storage
Industrial-scale batteries “can help ensure consistent dispatch, smoothing out load serving during on-peak periods by storing off-peak renewable wind power generation and supporting consistent baseload reliability and general grid reliability,” he explained. “Reshoring and the reindustrialization of the United States represent significant pent-up demand for batteries. Meanwhile, U.S. critical materials needs are likely to be reflected in policies that support mineral extraction and processing, as well as financial market dynamics that incentivize battery recycling.
At present, global battery manufacturing capacity is high, he added, but more capacity is planned.
“The bigger questions are where that capacity is located, how much will eventually come online, and whether there will be sufficient minerals and materials in secure supply chains to support future battery demand. Battery demand is likely to rise significantly over the next 10 years. Meeting that demand will require not only additional battery throughput, but also significant investment across the entire battery supply chain.”
As reported often in
Battery Technology
, the global nature of energy storage production and competition for raw materials and investment dollars is a moving target subject to geopolitical shifts and domestic imperatives. Schenker sees a battery manufacturing environment in which “the global supply chain for dual-use goods is bifurcating.
Related:
AI Continues to Rise in Battery Production, Slashing Test Times & Costs
The technological iron curtain
“A Technological Iron Curtain is falling, with the US and its allies on one side and China and its allies on the other side. It would not surprise me if there were a medium-term objective established to ensure, or at least strengthen, US battery self-sufficiency. This is likely to drive greater domestic capacity as well as more secure battery materials supply chains for the United States and US allies.”
So what’s Schenker’s best-case version for how battery manufacturing evolves in a manner that ensures sufficient and secure supplies of the minerals and materials the United States and U.S. allies will need?
“An ideal scenario would be sufficient battery manufacturing capacity to meet rising demand, supported by reliable US access to critical minerals and materials and greater battery recycling,” he concluded. “The challenge will be getting all of those pieces in place quickly enough to meet the significant demand opportunities ahead.”

title: Musk explains why Tesla Robotaxi is not running at night, and lidar is the answer
content:
Elon Musk
Tesla Robotaxi
Fred Lambert
| Oct 3 2026 - 7:36 am PT
Elon Musk says the main thing holding back Tesla Robotaxi’s night hours is that the cars have a hard time seeing pets in the dark. His example was “grey kittens on grey tarmac.”
That’s a low-light, low-contrast detection problem, which is the textbook weakness of cameras and the exact thing lidar and radar handle. Musk has spent years calling those sensors a “crutch” and a “fool’s errand.”
Robotaxi gets one more hour, and Musk explains why it’s only one
Late Friday night, Tesla’s Robotaxi account announced that the Austin service is “now available until 11pm.” Until now, it shut down at 10 PM.
Musk reposted the announcement and explained what’s keeping the cars off the road later than that:
“The main thing we’re trying to solve is making sure that we don’t run over pets when they’re hard to see at night. Literally trying to avoid grey kittens on grey tarmac in the dark.”
Robotaxi operating hours moved from 10pm to 11pm.
The main thing we’re trying to solve is making sure that we don’t run over pets when they’re hard to see at night. Literally trying to avoid grey kittens on grey tarmac in the dark.
https://t.co/y4HSVILLqd
Some context on that extra hour. When Tesla
launched Robotaxi in Austin in June 2025
, the app took ride requests from 6 AM to midnight. Fifteen months later, the service closes an hour earlier than it did on day one.
And it’s a small service. Tesla has barely scaled since launch, even with the addition of the Cybercabs last month.
Cameras need light and contrast. Lidar and radar don’t
A camera is a passive sensor. It works with whatever light bounces off an object, and it picks that object out by how much it stands apart from the background. A grey animal on grey pavement at night gives it very little of either.
Lidar is an active sensor. It fires its own laser pulses and times how long they take to come back, which gives the car a distance and a 3D shape for whatever is sitting on the road. It works the same at midnight as it does at noon, and it doesn’t need the kitten to be a different color than the asphalt. It needs the kitten to stick up from the road, and kittens, being 3D objects, tend to do that.
Radar does a similar job with radio waves and adds speed. It’s weaker on something that small, but it keeps working in the fog, dust and glare that blind cameras.
Every company running driverless cars at scale uses all three. Waymo’s sixth-generation system has 13 cameras, 4 lidars and 6 radars. In August,
Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov showed kids chasing dogs across a pitch-black street
, where the camera feed was close to useless and the lidar view was clean. Waymo’s roughly 4,000 driverless vehicles run 24 hours a day.
Tesla went the other way. It
removed radar from its cars in May 2021
, dropped ultrasonic sensors in 2022, and has never shipped a car with lidar.
Musk’s record on lidar and night vision
Musk in April 2019: “Lidar is a fool’s errand. Anyone relying on lidar is doomed.”
In February 2022, he called lidar “a seductive local maximum” and said a general solution to self-driving “necessarily will require silicon neural nets & cameras.”
In August 2025, he went further and claimed that “lidar and radar reduce safety due to sensor contention.”
And in May of this year, he posted a “photon count reconstruction” image from Tesla’s cameras and wrote: “This is why Tesla FSD can see so well at night or through extreme glare.”
That was five months ago, and now seeing at night is “the main thing” Tesla is trying to solve.
He knew the trade-off all along. When Tesla was pulling radar in 2021,
Musk told Electrek in direct messages that “vision with high-res radar would be better than pure vision.”
And NHTSA is currently
investigating 3.2 million Teslas over FSD crashes in low-visibility conditions
, a probe in which it demanded an internal Tesla document titled “Radar Saves Us.”
Electrek’s Take
Musk wrote that post like Tesla just found a new problem. It didn’t. Cameras losing dark, low-contrast objects at night is the oldest limitation in the book, and it’s why everyone else put lidar and radar on their cars. Ten years ago this month, Tesla said every car it built had the hardware for full self-driving. Its CEO is figuring out in October 2026 that grey things are hard to see in the dark.
And Musk picked the cutest example available. The same physics applies to a tire tread on the highway or a kid in a black hoodie. Those are bigger and easier to spot, but nobody should want the safety margin to be “bigger than a kitten.”
To be fair, no sensor suite gets this to zero. A Waymo ran over a bodega cat in San Francisco last October, and Waymo said it darted under the car as it pulled away. But Tesla is the only one whose CEO says the cars have trouble seeing the animal in the first place.
The cost excuse is gone too. Rivian
said this week that lidar now costs it “a few hundred dollars”
per vehicle.
What bothers us most is the part Musk skipped. The sun sets a little after 7 PM in Austin right now, so Tesla’s Robotaxis are already driving in the dark every night with a problem he says isn’t solved. And customer Teslas run “Full Self-Driving” on the same cameras at any hour, with no curfew.
Tesla is now one update away from getting back to its launch-day midnight closing time. Waymo, with lidar and radar on every car, never closes. How many more one-hour updates before Tesla admits there’s a sensor for that?

title: I tried taking the budget-priced Ride1Up Roadster V3 e-bike off-roading. Here's what happened next
content:
Micah Toll
| Oct 3 2026 - 6:26 am PT
Ride1Up Roadster V3
is, for all intents and purposes, is a budget-focused daily driver urban bike. It’s not really a gravel bike. Maybe if you stand back a bit and squint, you could give it a bit more of a gravel bike interpretation. But ultimately, it’s a lightweight, affordable urban e-bike with decent multi-role tires that I mostly use for cruising around bike lanes and city streets.
So naturally, yesterday I took it on a 38 km (24 mile) ride where I spent most of the time off-road.
And you know what? The little
$1,295 e-bike
surprised me.
My route included just about every type of surface I probably wouldn’t have chosen when pulling a metro bike out of my quiver of e-bikes: gravel roads, hard-packed dirt, loose sandy trails, muddy puddles, and even a few rocky climbs thrown in for good measure.
The ride started with a train trip north of the city, which immediately highlighted one of the
Roadster V3’s
biggest advantages: it’s light. Compared to the
70- or 80-pound fat-tire e-bikes
that have become increasingly common, getting the Roadster through the train station, onto the train, and even holding it securely on escalators in the stations was refreshingly easy. It tips the scales at 40 lb (18 kg) stock, though the extra rack and bags I installed, not to mention the dropper seat post, probably add a couple of extra pounds to that total.
That train maneuverability might not sound like much of an “off-road” feature, but for real-world adventure riding, being able to easily combine a bike with public transportation or lift it into a truck to get to the trails can open up a lot more interesting routes.
Once I left the train station and got rolling, I kept the bike in Eco mode basically the entire time, taking advantage of the MiVice torque sensor that provides super natural power application – like the bikes is just an extension of your legs.
The Roadster V3 isn’t an overly powerful e-bike, and that’s actually part of what I like about it. It feels much more like riding a bicycle that happens to have an electric tailwind than riding a small motorcycle with pedals attached.
That was especially true off-road. I was still putting in plenty of effort, but the motor was there to take the edge off when things got tougher.
There were a couple of climbs where I realized a little too late that I was in too high of a gear. Instead of grinding nearly to a halt while trying to downshift under load, I gave the Roadster’s hidden throttle a quick blip to keep my momentum while I sorted myself out. It gave me the chance to let my own power off the pedals for a few seconds and downshift without losing too much speed.
That’s basically how I prefer to use a throttle on this kind of e-bike: not as the primary means of propulsion, but as an occasional little electric get-out-of-jail-free card. It happens a lot when I need to squirt out away from cars in the city, but the same benefits apply when I need a little extra help on a rocky ascent or to power through a section of deep sand.
And speaking of sand, the biggest challenge was definitely all of that sand.
The harder-packed sand sections of trails were fine, but some sections were fairly loose, and the Roadster’s relatively narrow Continental 700x45c tires obviously aren’t going to float over sand like a four-inch fat tire.
I could feel the bike starting to wander sideways underneath me a few times, which definitely got my attention. But with a little finesse, some momentum, and perhaps a healthy amount of optimism, I managed to keep the rubber side down and my feet on the pedals. Though again, installing
that dropper seat post
was quite helpful when I got to a more technical section and wanted to be sure I could easily and safely tap toes on the ground if it came to that, then pop the seat back up to proper pedal position as soon as I passed the obstacles – all without stopping or dismounting the bike.
Whenever back on the gravel and harder-packed dirt, though, the bike felt right at home. Even the occasional rocky sections were manageable as long as I remembered what I was riding and picked my lines accordingly.
It had also drizzled a few hours before I started, leaving several puddles scattered along the route. Here, the Roadster V3 had another surprisingly useful advantage over many purpose-built gravel bikes: fenders.
There’s something wonderfully practical about blasting through a puddle and not immediately painting a stripe of muddy water up your back.
After 38 km (24 miles) and around 1 hour and 50 minutes of riding, I rolled back home with roughly a third of the battery remaining. That was particularly impressive considering how much of the ride involved sand, dirt, climbing, and other conditions that tend to make an electric motor work harder.
Granted, when I stick to the city, I generally get around 70 km (44 miles) per charge, but riding through sand has a way of eating battery like nothing else. I’d call an extrapolated range of 57 km or 35 miles in off-road conditions pretty good, at least for a relatively small 360Wh battery.
Of course, part of that range came from the fact that I was working pretty hard, too.
My Garmin watch estimated that I burned 696 calories during the ride. I always take smartwatch calorie estimates with a grain of salt, but my legs certainly agreed with the general assessment. This wasn’t a ride where I sat back and let the motor haul me around. I was pedaling hard, choosing gears, maintaining momentum, and using the electric assist to supplement my effort rather than replace it.
And that might be my biggest takeaway from the whole experiment.
If your idea of an e-bike is something you expect to throttle around on without contributing much yourself, the Roadster V3 probably isn’t the machine I’d choose for a 38 km mixed-terrain adventure. It does have that stealth throttle, but it’s not a powerhouse and it’s not a motorcycle.
But if you’re a cycling-friendly e-biker who likes doing much of the work yourself and simply wants some assistance to flatten hills, fight headwinds, or get through tougher sections, it works remarkably well.
Would I recommend the Roadster V3 as a dedicated gravel e-bike? Probably not, at least not in this variant.
There’s a suspended version with a suspension fork
that would help a bit, but there are bikes with wider tires, more aggressive geometry, and components specifically designed for dedicated gravel riding jobs.
But that’s also what made this ride so much fun, seeing how versatile my daily driver urban bike can be when I push it.
This is the same relatively inexpensive e-bike I can ride through the city, carry onto a train without throwing out my back, commute on without looking like I’m preparing for the Dakar Rally, and then apparently spend nearly two hours bouncing through dirt, gravel, sand, rocks, and puddles.
And it got me home with battery to spare.
For $1,295
, I’d call that a pretty successful adventure.

title: FedEx believes $300M electric truck spend will save them $800M in diesel
content:
Commercial EVs
Harbinger Motors
Jo Borrás
| Oct 3 2026 - 5:54 am PT
In a record-setting commercial truck deal, international shipping giant FedEx has placed an order for 2,000 all-electric box trucks from American startup Harbinger in a deal that’s reportedly worth more than $300 million – but the ROI could be
FedEx is making serious moves to fully electrify its operating fleet by 2040, and this latest Harbinger deal is believed to be one of the largest binding orders for electric medium or heavy-duty trucks in history.
It’s certainly Harbinger’s largest order
, at least!
“FedEx is demonstrating that the business case for incorporating electric vehicles into real-world fleet operations at scale makes sense,” said John Harris, Co-Founder and CEO, Harbinger. “
Our previous work together gave FedEx firsthand experience with the performance and economic advantages Harbinger vehicles can deliver
. We are proud that a global leader like FedEx is turning its sustainability goals into action by choosing Harbinger to help expand its electric fleet.”
Let’s do the math
FedEx electric box van; by Harbinger.
Harbinger estimates that each of the electric Class 5 and 6 medium-duty box trucks delivered will reduce FedEx’ fuel costs by around $20,000 annually compared with the conventional diesel-powered vehicle they replace. Additionally,
Harbinger says its vehicles are designed for a functional service life of 20 years
2,000 trucks x $20,000 in fuel savings per year x 20 years. That works out to $800 million in total savings, for a
whopping
~166% ROI.
“Electrifying a fleet at this scale requires vehicles that can perform the work our robust operations demand while also delivering meaningful economic benefits,” said Paul Melander, Senior Vice President Safety & Transportation, FedEx and member of Harbinger’s Board of Directors. “Expanding our deployment of Harbinger vehicles gives us an opportunity to continue making progress toward our fleet electrification goals while reducing fuel and operating costs.”
Saving money is great, but the much more important issue for you and me is that the move to Harbinger electric trucks will help FedEx avoid more than 1.7 million tons of CO2 emissions over their projected operating lives – and that is a real win.

in the wake of their big EREV reveal at Work Truck Week earlier this year in Indiana
. I’ve included a Spotify link to that HEP-isode is included, below, but you can check it out on

title: Watt's up, doc? Huddig hybrid loader gets a big battery boost [video]
content:
Commercial EVs
Electric Heavy Machinery
Jo Borrás
| Oct 3 2026 - 4:58 am PT
Swedish heavy equipment brand HUDDIG has given its 1370 hybrid wheel loader platform a major battery upgrade for the new model year, boosting its battery capacity from 44 kWh to fully 61 kWh – an impressive, 40% upgrade!
HUDDIG’s 1370 TIGON hybrid is an incredibly flexible machine that can be equipped for a wide range of work.
In addition to being able to do everything a conventional wheel loader can do
, it can be fitted with a loader-mounted crane (LCC), a bucket lift with an insulated basket, and even be operated via remote control. The killer app for this machine, though, is a high-capacity traction battery that enables the loader to operate as a fully electric machine.
And this isn’t a gimmick or a concept for HUDDIG
, either – the company has a deployed fleet of 41 first-generation machines that had collectively operated for 96,306 hours and saved an estimated 140,439 gallons of diesel before the launch of the second-gen machine.
With 100,000 hours of actual operation
, we’ve had a very solid foundation for our development work,” says Daniel Åkerström, design engineer at Huddig. “The larger battery makes it possible to run on electric power even more, and we therefore expect to be able to improve these figures even further with the TIGON G2 HUDDIG.”
1370 TIGON G2
1370 TIGON G2; by HUDDIG.
For its second act, HUDDIG is giving the 1370 hybrid wheel loader platform a 40% bigger battery
regenerative braking, enabling operators to recover electrical energy while braking, driving downhill, or even lowering the boom.
That doesn’t mean the G2 will just spend 40% more time spent running on electric power – it’s a substantially bigger cut in fuel use when the G1 was
running on pure electric power nearly 60% of the time.
“The combination of extended electric runtime and more attachment options makes the Tigon G2 even more versatile and provides greater freedom to adapt the machine to the job at hand,” says Daniel Myrgren, marketing and sales manager at HUDDIG. “
The electric powertrain can also provide a clear competitive advantage in jobs where low emissions and low noise levels are becoming increasingly important
You can check out the official HUDDIG walk-around video, below, then let us know what you think of this hybrid hybrid equipment asset in the comments.

title: Battery storage paired with 37% of new U.S. residential solar systems in 2025 - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Battery storage was paired with 37% of new U.S. residential solar installations in 2025, up from 25% a year earlier, with adoption accelerating both in California and across other states.
MaryElizabeth Q. Mooney
03 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
More than one-third of new residential solar installations in the United States included battery storage in 2025, as batteries increasingly shift from an optional addition to a standard component of rooftop solar projects.
Battery storage was paired with 37% of new residential photovoltaic systems in 2025, up from 25% in 2024, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s latest
U.S. Distributed Solar and Storage Data
annual dataset
includes roughly 5.3 million distributed solar and solar-plus-storage systems installed through the end of 2025. That includes about 450,000 systems installed during 2025, representing an estimated 93% of the U.S. distributed solar market for the year.
California remains a major driver of the trend
About 74% of new residential solar installations in California included storage in 2025, up from 58% in 2024. But battery adoption also accelerated outside the state. Across all other states in Berkeley Lab’s comparison, the residential storage attachment rate climbed from 7% to 17% in one year.
Berkeley Lab highlighted particularly large increases in Arizona and Texas. Hawaii and California continued to post the highest residential storage attachment rates in the country.
California’s rise in solar-plus-storage installations follows the state’s transition to its Net Billing Tariff, commonly called NEM 3.0, in April 2023. The policy reduced the value of electricity exported by new rooftop solar customers during many hours, increasing the value of storing excess daytime generation for later use.
That change quickly altered the composition of California’s rooftop solar market.
More than half of California solar customers were pairing batteries with their systems
, up from about 20% in October 2023.
Growth is no longer limited to California
Battery attachment rates outside California
more than doubled from 2024 to 2025
. Berkeley Lab did not attribute that increase to any single factor, but installers in other markets are increasingly confronting changes to net-metering structures and time-of-use electricity rates that can increase the value of consuming stored solar power rather than exporting it.
Storage adoption also increased in the non-residential market, although it remains far below residential levels. Batteries were attached to 11% of U.S. non-residential solar installations in 2025, up from 7% in 2024. California’s non-residential attachment rate increased from 12% to 18%, while the rate across all other states doubled from 4% to 8%.
The typical amount of energy stored in residential batteries did not change significantly. Median residential storage capacity remained 13.5 kWh in both 2024 and 2025.
However, the power those systems can deliver increased sharply. Median discharge capacity increased from 6 kW in 2024 to 11.4 kW in 2025. Berkeley Lab attributed much of that increase to growing deployment of the Tesla Powerwall 3, which has higher discharge capacity than previous versions.
The report cautions that its attachment rates do not capture the entire distributed storage market. They exclude batteries added later to existing solar installations as well as standalone battery systems.
That means the data measure how often installers pair batteries with new solar projects, rather than the full rate of residential battery deployment. Even under that narrower definition, the year-over-year increase suggests solar-plus-storage is rapidly becoming a larger part of the U.S. residential market.

title: Brazil hits 56 GW of connection headroom for battery auctions - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Brazil’s available grid capacity for battery storage projects exceeds the association’s estimate of 2028-30 power needs by up to 12.5 times, according to an analysis of transmission data.
Lívia Neves
03 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Brazil has about 56 GW of remaining grid connection capacity for battery energy storage systems (BESS) participating in the December capacity reserve auctions, according to a calculation by the Brazilian Association of Energy Storage Solutions (Absae) based on Technical Note 0095/2026 from the National Electric System Operator (ONS).
The estimated headroom is 5.6 to 12.5 times the association’s projected power shortfall for 2028 to 2030, which ranges from 4.5 GW to 10 GW. At the substations receiving preferential treatment under MME Ordinance No. 136/2026, aggregate connection headroom reaches about 13.7 GW, exceeding even the higher end of the estimated shortfall.
The technical note, published on Sept. 30, measures remaining capacity at different points on the grid for storage systems that may participate in the Capacity Reserve Auctions scheduled for Dec. 2 and 4.
Absae said the distribution of connection headroom across different regions reduces the risk of widespread grid connection constraints for projects competing in the auctions. The association’s executive director, Fabio Lima, said the network has about 56 GW of available capacity, well above the power requirement it estimates for coming years, with capacity distributed across several regions.
Of the 129 substations designated for preferential treatment in the auctions, 93 have available connection capacity, according to Absae. They are concentrated mainly in the states of Bahia, Piauí, and Ceará, as well as northern Minas Gerais, with individual blocks of capacity of up to about 3.7 GW.
Some locations have smaller amounts of headroom or capacity shared among different substations, while others have no available capacity because of physical-space, short-circuit, or construction-schedule constraints.
Connection availability is considered when projects are ranked by substation, subarea, and area under the auction rules.
Substations designated as strategic under MME Ordinance No. 136/2026 receive a 10% bonus in their ranking price. The measure is intended to encourage battery installations at locations where they can provide additional grid services.
Absae said the systems planned for the auctions could operate as grid-forming assets and contribute to voltage stability. At these locations, storage could reduce the need for equipment that provides electrical support, such as synchronous condensers.
Connection headroom at non-preferred substations totals about 36 GW, according to the association’s calculation. Projects at these locations can also compete in the auctions, increasing the pool of potentially eligible developments.
Brazil’s Energy Research Office (EPE) received registrations for 6,091 projects for the auctions, totaling 296.8 GW of capacity.
The number ultimately qualified will be lower after technical analysis and the application of connection constraints, but Absae expects the number of eligible projects to remain significantly above the amount of capacity to be contracted.
The association said the combination of the connection headroom identified by ONS and the large number of registered projects should maintain competition among bidders. Lima also said adherence to the auction schedule demonstrates the sector’s commitment to meeting the deadlines and that the large number of registered projects should make price the main differentiator between bids, benefiting consumers.

title: The case for railway-integrated solar in South Korea - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
South Korea’s extensive railway network could provide new space for solar generation in densely populated areas where land availability is limited. Researchers have investigated the potential of installing PV systems between railway tracks, finding that suitable sections of five surface railway corridors could host more than 8.5 MW of solar capacity.
Lior Kahana
03 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
An international research team has investigated the potential of installing PV systems between railway tracks in South Korea as a way to expand solar generation without competing for scarce land. The researchers found that suitable sections of five surface railway corridors could host more than 8.5 MW of PV capacity, highlighting the potential of existing transport infrastructure to support solar deployment in densely populated areas.
“Dense metropolitan regions need renewable energy strategies that do not compete for land. Railway corridors offer one such option because they already occupy linear public space and connect closely to traction and distribution infrastructure,” the researchers said.
“Our study examines whether the transport system can use PV electricity generated within railway corridors, how much electricity must be exported or curtailed, what storage capacity is needed, and how financial uncertainty affects the probability of payback,” they added.
The researchers assessed five surface railway corridors: the Gaya and Donghae lines in Busan, above-ground sections of Seoul Subway Line 1 and Daegu Metro Line 1, and selected open sections of the Gyeongbu Line, which connects Seoul and Busan.
Using OpenStreetMap railway geometry and a Korean digital surface model in QGIS, the researchers excluded tunnels, viaducts and track sections with annual shading losses exceeding 15%.
They simulated the installation of 1.05-meter-wide flexible monocrystalline silicon laminates, with a minimum clearance of 150 mm from the railhead on each side. The laminates had a nominal efficiency of 21.4% and a power density of 214 W/m².
The simulations assumed soiling losses of 3.5%, including an additional percentage point to account for railway dust, as well as combined mismatch and DC wiring losses of 2%. The researchers also assumed inverter efficiency of 97.5% and an albedo of 0.18 for ballast and concrete sleepers. They validated the generation model against 17 months of measured rooftop PV production in Busan.
The group then simulated railway PV output and matched it against hourly traction-demand profiles to calculate self-consumption, grid exports and curtailment. It also compared centralized and distributed electrical connection configurations and assessed lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery capacities of up to 2 kWh per kilowatt of installed PV capacity.
The researchers evaluated the system’s financial performance over 20 years, assuming annual PV module degradation of 0.45%. They conducted sensitivity analysis and a 10,000-run Monte Carlo simulation to account for financial uncertainty.
“The screening identified 28.4 km of suitable surface railway corridor and 39,760 m² of installable area. This corresponds to 8.51 MW of photovoltaic capacity, based on the corrected module density of 4.67 m²/kW for a 1,435 mm standard-gauge corridor,” the researchers said.
They estimated annual generation at 9.95 GWh, with a capacity-weighted capacity factor of 13.4%. Without storage, 62.3% of PV generation coincided with traction demand. Of the remaining 37.7%, 19.8% could be exported to the grid and 17.8% would be curtailed.
The researchers found that a 0.5 kWh/kW battery could reduce the unabsorbed surplus from about 38% to 8.5% of generation. Adding the battery would increase the levelized cost of electricity by about 10% when round-trip storage losses are charged against delivered energy. Before accounting for those losses, the increase would be 9.0%.
“The probabilistic analysis yields a median levelised cost of energy (LCOE) of 170 USD/MWh on a delivered-energy basis and a 68% probability of payback within 12 years with a 40% capital subsidy, compared with roughly one-third without a subsidy,” the researchers concluded.
The findings are presented in the study “
Climate-resilient urban energy infrastructure through rail-integrated photovoltaics in land-constrained South Korea
,” published in
Engineering Science and Technology, an International Journal
The research team included scientists from Dong-A University and Kyungsung University in South Korea, the Sumatra Institute of Technology in Indonesia, and the Higher Colleges of Technology in the United Arab Emirates.

title: Middle market momentum - pv magazine Global
content: Tell us about Clean Capital’s business model and how it operates in the community solar space. We’re about 10 years old, and originally we started buying operating assets and working with a pool of investors over time. Today, we’re backed by Manulife Investment Company. As an IPP, we acquire, develop, and own assets across 26 states and we’re in what’s called the “middle market.” Community solar, commercial and industrial (C&I), behind-the-meter, front-of-the-meter. We serve a lot of manufacturing facilities and municipalities’ power needs. When you’re doing utility scale, that focuses the company on one big project. We are very dispersed in terms of our projects, which allows us to play in a lot of different places and do things in more manageable chunks. Every state is different. For example, revenue for batteries in New York is different from revenue in Massachusetts, which is way different from Texas. What’s interesting to me about Texas is that it is now one of the fastest-growing solar markets in the US and we’re seeing a lot of deployment. You’re also seeing political leadership that doesn’t support it. How is demand for distributed generation solar right now? The conversation around things like tariffs and tax credits is very centralized and we have to think about what’s actually happening at state level, where they’re having to live with the consequences of these federal decisions. We are not a centrally managed economy; the White House can cut a deal on something, but it still has to get permitted at a local level. And people are saying “wait a moment, let’s hold up and decide what’s best in our backyard.” After passing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act the government immediately started tweeting about energy affordability, because they knew they were causing an affordability crisis by making it harder to bring on new renewables. Big picture, for a second: you have a scaling energy demand in the US for the first time in decades at the level we’re seeing, and not enough supply to meet that. That delta is causing utilities to increase their rates, and we’re beginning to see those increases on people’s bills. Just as we’re feeling the crunch, instead of adding to the supply this administration is trying to temper down any type of renewables. The supply-demand issue affects us as well, because it determines where we can develop and the conversations we’re having at a local level. But as the price of electricity is going up, we can come with solid, affordable power that people can take long-term contracts on, providing them with a way to solve the challenges they’re facing from a budgeting perspective, which is a much different conversation from the ones we were having 10 years ago around ESG. Big bills, ugly prices During the first half of 2026, utility companies in the United States requested $18.6 billion in electric and gas rate increases, according to a report by US non-profit PowerLines. The organization’s data showed utilities filed $9.2 billion in rate increase requests during the second quarter of 2026 – enough to potentially affect future bills for more than 56 million customers. More than two in three consumers reported their electric or gas bills increased in 2026, and more than three in four said they are concerned their bills will keep rising. Southern states were worst affected, followed by the Midwest, Western and then Northeastern states. Meanwhile, a July 2026 report from Lazard showed renewables remain the lowest-cost new-build generation based on levelized cost of energy (LCOE). Gas generation is set to get more expensive, with wait times for new peaker plants already very long. Attitudes to solar obviously vary from national to state level, but is it becoming more bipartisan as people see its benefits? In many states right now, the top issue is electricity pricing and affordability. As we get into this affordability conversation there’s a lot of debate happening at the state level, especially ahead of midterm elections (in November 2026) and presidential elections (in 2028). For a long time, solar was part of the climate conversation and it was “the right thing to do.” While that’s a nice story to tell, I think now where we have to transition as an industry, it’s talking about the economic impact. We should be talking about jobs, affordability, because that’s where the focus is right now, and I think the industry is adjusting to that both in light of a federal administration that is not friendly to our technology and also recognizing that people don’t understand the difference between utility scale, distributed generation, any of that. All they want to do is plug their phone in and charge it at a reasonable rate in their house. I gave a tour the other day at one of our sites next to a long-haul trucking facility and there was a guy who worked there sitting at the gate with me. And when he found out I worked in solar, he pulled up his electricity bill on his phone and we started talking about generation, transmission and all that stuff. He said he had no idea what any of that meant three months ago but because his bills are getting outrageous he’s beginning to understand. That’s part of a wider movement. I heard an interview with [US environmental activist and author] Bill McKibben recently and he has a great framework, which is that solar used to be the Whole Foods of the energy industry and now it’s the Costco. But we could capitalize on this momentum even faster. And as an industry we need to get better at communicating. We need to be in the room with policymakers and educate them. For us, that state-level policy game is really where a lot of the fight is at. It’s how do you permit projects; can you net meter your solar? Is there a community solar program? Being able to understand and navigate that complex space is really challenging and this provides us with a market opportunity. The post Middle market momentum appeared first on pv magazine Global .

title: US Task Force 401 taps drone defenses that autonomously classify threats
content: Digital Force Technologies (DFT) has secured a US contract to supply counter-drone systems that combine sensor data, autonomous threat assessment and engagement capabilities in a single software-driven architecture. The San Diego-based company announced the $500 million Indefinite Delivery, Indefinite Quantity (IDIQ) award from Joint Interagency Task Force 401 on September 29. It supports the task force’s Domestic Shield program, which aims to accelerate layered drone defenses for military installations, critical assets and personnel. DFT will provide its counter-unmanned aerial systems and counter-small unmanned aerial systems capabilities for force protection, base defense and counter-drone operations. The contract covers requirements within the continental United States and overseas. Sensor fusion at the tactical edge At the center of DFT’s systems is SeraphimOS, an edge-based software architecture designed to combine information from multiple sensors. According to the company, it autonomously assesses and classifies threats while delivering actionable information to operators in real time. The architecture brings sensing, decision-making and action together at the tactical edge. Its intended role is to help operators respond to drone threats while accommodating changes in equipment and mission requirements. “This award represents a significant milestone for DFT and reinforces the importance of rapidly delivering adaptable, mission-ready technology to the warfighter,” said Justin MacLaurin, President and CEO of Digital Force Technologies. “The UAS threat is evolving at an extraordinary pace, and defending our forces and critical infrastructure requires systems that can evolve just as quickly.” Open architecture connects sensors and effectors SeraphimOS uses an open architecture that supports integration with sensors, effectors, platforms and third-party systems. DFT said this allows it to configure capabilities for specific missions without requiring a closed technology stack supplied by a single vendor. That flexibility is central to the company’s approach as drone threats change. Operators can integrate new sensing and engagement capabilities as their requirements evolve. “Our SeraphimOS -powered mission systems bring sensing, decision and action together at the tactical edge, giving operators the flexibility to integrate new sensors, effectors and capabilities as the mission changes,” MacLaurin said. For counter-drone missions , the platform supports detection, tracking and identification through engagement using kinetic and non-kinetic effects. DFT also said SeraphimOS enables advanced orchestration of uncrewed systems. This includes coordinated sensing across multiple domains and autonomous operations in contested, disconnected, and degraded environments. Domestic Shield targets layered protection The award supports Domestic Shield ’s push to deploy layered counter-drone capabilities against rapidly evolving unmanned aerial threats. The initiative focuses on protecting military installations, critical assets and personnel. “Safeguarding our critical assets against increasingly agile drone threats demands flexible, highly mobile protection that can deploy rapidly where it is needed most,” said U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, director of Joint Interagency Task Force 401. “By continuing to provide capabilities on the marketplace through a streamlined framework, JIATF-401 is able to cut through red tape and rapidly deliver state-of-the-art counter-UAS solutions into the hands of warfighters,” he added . The announcement describes the systems’ intended capabilities but does not provide detection ranges, engagement distances, or performance results. It also does not specify deployment quantities or individual delivery orders under the IDIQ contract.

title: Tiny rice-sized GaN chip packs 3x more power, 20x better signals
content: Northrop Grumman has unveiled a new gallium nitride chip aimed at handling demanding radio-frequency workloads with less hardware.The FORTITUDE™ chip can combine signal switching and filtering inside a single device. Northrop Grumman says it delivers three times more power and 20 times better signal quality.That performance could matter across systems that operate in crowded or interference-heavy environments. The company lists satellites, radar, GPS, electronic warfare, and future 6G networks among potential applications.GaN gets new structureThe chip is also small enough to fit within a package roughly the size of a grain of rice. Its compact footprint could help engineers reduce weight and power demands inside larger systems.FORTITUDE uses a patented gallium nitride structure built from multiple ultra-thin layers. Northrop Grumman describes the architecture as a “superlattice.” The stacked layers control electron movement through the semiconductor while increasing charge density.The company says the structure can carry about 10 times the charge of standard GaN chips. That higher density helps the device handle more electrical power without simply increasing its physical size.Heat management also becomes important as RF hardware pushes higher power levels. The superlattice design aims to reduce energy losses during operation. The approach comes from years of Northrop Grumman research into microelectronics. The technology was previously known as the Super Lattice Castellated Field Effect Transistor.Switching and filtering togetherMost RF systems rely on multiple components to manipulate signals as they move through a circuit. FORTITUDE puts two important functions into the same semiconductor.The device can switch signals at subnanosecond speeds while filtering unwanted frequencies. That combination lets it shape electrical signals before they reach other parts of a system.Northrop Grumman says FORTITUDE can operate across frequencies ranging from kilohertz levels to 20 GHz. That broad range could support multiple radar and communications bands with fewer specialized components. The company says the chip can replace dozens of components in some system architectures. That could reduce weight and simplify the electronics surrounding the RF chain.More signal in crowded spectrumModern RF systems increasingly operate alongside other transmitters and sources of interference. Military platforms face particularly demanding conditions when several electronic systems compete for spectrum.FORTITUDE is designed to maintain cleaner signal performance under those conditions. Northrop Grumman says its architecture can deliver clearer data while consuming less power.The technology also targets commercial systems. Future communications networks could place greater demands on RF hardware as operators move toward higher frequencies and more complex signal environments.Northrop Grumman is developing FORTITUDE for both defense and commercial markets in the United States. Its potential applications span communications, sensing, and electronic warfare.The engineering challenge remains familiar even as the hardware changes. More information needs to move through increasingly crowded electromagnetic environments. FORTITUDE tackles that problem at the semiconductor level, combining more power and signal control inside a much smaller piece of hardware.
