title: Scientists Simulated Moons Being Blown Apart – and Found Something Unexpected
content:
Many icy moons around the outer planets may have been struck by other large objects early in their histories, with some impacts energetic enough to break the moons apart completely. Credit: Shutterstock
A study suggests that icy moons can still harbor oceans after catastrophic collisions, a finding that could help guide the search for life beyond Earth.
Many moons orbiting Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are thought to conceal liquid water beneath miles of icy shell. These buried oceans hold a basic ingredient for life as we know it, making them promising places to search for extraterrestrial organisms in a region shaped by violent collisions.
Scientists suspect some of today’s moons are reassembled remnants that were repeatedly shattered by space debris and pulled back together. This cosmic demolition derby raises a critical question for astrobiologists: Do massive collisions destroy a moon’s ocean and extinguish any chance for life?
A University of Maryland-led study, published in
Nature Astronomy
, investigated that question by following simulated moons through destruction, reassembly, and billions of years of subsequent evolution.
“The big question we asked was whether these destructions help moons have oceans afterward or whether they delete the ocean and reset the moon into a cold, dead world,” explained lead author Marc Neveu, an astronomy associate research scientist at the University of Maryland. “What we found was that those big collisions don’t really matter as far as oceans are concerned. If there was an ocean before, there’s likely to be an ocean after and vice versa.”
Cracks, canyons, craters and streaks are seen in this image of Saturn’s icy moon, Dione. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
Did a collision soften Rhea’s craters?
Although a collision might not determine whether an ocean exists, the heat it delivers could still leave visible traces on a moon’s surface. On Saturn’s moon Rhea, ancient craters look unusually smooth and softened. The researchers see those features as a possible opportunity to test whether an impact warmed an existing ocean enough to alter the ice above it.
“It’s like building a snowman in the winter, and then a week later, there’s been warming and sunlight so the snowman is melting away,” Neveu explained. “Rhea’s craters look smoothed out like that, but it wasn’t the sun. The heat came from below. A long-ago collision that boosted an interior ocean could help explain why the moon appears that way.”
Shattered moons can remain ocean worlds
Following a collision’s effects over such long periods required more than a model of the crash itself. Neveu and his colleagues at the Southwest Research Institute in Colorado and the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel connected simulations of impacts with a separate model of how a moon’s interior evolves. Together, the models could show both what happened when a moon broke apart and whether the rebuilt world retained enough heat to sustain liquid water.
The impact simulations tracked millions of rock and ice fragments as they shattered, heated up, and clumped back together. The team modeled moons with radii of roughly 500 and 1,000 kilometers, or about 310 and 620 miles, struck by smaller space rocks with enough force to blow them apart.
“These simulations were pretty much the biggest collisions we could come up with,” Neveu said. “If those didn’t make a difference, it’s unlikely smaller ones would either.”
Diagram depicting how collisions may destroy moons and impact their reformation. Credit: Marc Neveu, University of Maryland
The interior model then followed the reassembled moons for 4.5 billion years, calculating how heat built up and escaped from their cores and whether ice could melt into an ocean. This longer view revealed why an impact’s effects depended on the moon’s size. The crash supplied heat, but it also rearranged the rock and ice, changing how effectively the rebuilt moon could hold on to its warmth.
“In larger moons, the energy of the crash converts into extra heat that can actually thicken up an existing ocean for a couple billion years. In smaller moons, the story flips,” Neveu said. “Before a collision, these small moons keep a jumbled outer layer of mixed ice and rock that acts like an insulating blanket, helping trap the warmth that sustains an ocean. The impact shakes everything apart, and when the moon re-forms, the rock sinks to the center and the ice floats to the top. It gets harder for the smaller moon to keep an ocean because the blanket’s gone, but in neither case did a collision create an ocean that would’ve otherwise stayed frozen.”
Heat from tides also influences whether water stays liquid beneath the ice. As gravity deforms a moon, it can generate warmth inside, and Neveu cautioned that this process matters at least as much as collision history when considering a moon’s potential to support life. Changes in moons’ orbits can also set them on collision courses, so reconstructing their past requires connecting their movements with what happens beneath their surfaces.
“Down the line, I would love to press play on a moon system and watch how the moons move, how they smash into each other and how their interiors change as a result,” Neveu said. “Maybe then we can reconstruct what happened around Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.”
Hunting for life inside rebuilt moons
The findings apply to numerous worlds that NASA and other space agencies plan to investigate, including Saturn’s mid-sized moons Mimas, Enceladus, Tethys, Dione, and Rhea. They also apply to Uranus’s moons Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon, and Neptune’s large moon Triton.
Knowing which of these worlds are most likely to harbor water could help NASA and the planetary science community choose spacecraft destinations and decide what instruments should look for. A buried ocean might reveal itself through its gravitational effects, while salty deposits or icy volcanoes called cryovolcanoes could provide clues at the surface. Expectations about the life an ocean might support would also shape the sensitivity needed to detect it.
“If there’s only a handful of microbes, you won’t be designing the same kind of search mission as you would if the ocean were full of whales,” Neveu said. “The type of life we’re looking for will determine what kind of tools we need to develop.”
Reference: “The role of disruptive impacts on ocean generation and longevity in icy moons” by Marc Neveu, Raluca Rufu, Alyssa Rhoden, Kevin J. Walsh and Yuval Steinberg, 20 August 2026,
Nature Astronomy

title: FDA Approves First Drug To Treat Alexander Disease After 30 Years of Research
content:
Alexander disease is a rare, progressive genetic disorder of the nervous system that damages myelin and disrupts normal brain function. Credit: Shutterstock
The drug is the first and only treatment that can change the course of this rare neurological disease.
For decades, patients diagnosed with Alexander disease had no options beyond managing their symptoms. The ultra-rare, progressive, and often fatal neurological disorder affects fewer than one in a million people worldwide. It affects motor and cognitive abilities, along with automatic bodily functions such as heart rate and breathing.
Symptoms can include seizures, loss of developmental skills, mobility challenges, eating and speaking difficulties, and increased pressure in the brain.
Now, the Food and Drug Administration has approved Zanvastro, the first drug that directly targets the underlying disease process.
During clinical trials, patients taking Zanvastro for just over a year had significantly better walking speeds than untreated patients. Motor function stabilized, and in some cases, it improved. The newly approved drug is administered by a trained healthcare professional as an injection into the spinal canal every three months. It will be available in the United States in the coming weeks, while use in other countries will occur through a licensing agreement between its developer, Ionis Pharmaceuticals, and the Italian pharmaceutical company Recordati.
In Alexander disease, GFAP protein (shown here in green) gathers and clumps in brain cells called astrocytes. An individual astrocyte, dyed red, is shown at center, and nuclei from astrocytes, neurons, and other cells are dyed blue. Credit: Tracy Hagemann
Ionis began the human trial in the summer of 2021, evaluating the treatment’s efficacy and safety in 54 patients at 13 sites worldwide. The FDA approval covers patients from infancy through adulthood. Alexander disease can first appear at any point across that age range, with symptoms that vary depending on when it begins.
Albee Messing. Credit: University of Wisconsin-Madison
“This is a wonderful and long-awaited day for the Alexander disease community,” says Albee Messing, professor emeritus of comparative biosciences at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and former director of its Waisman Center.
An accidental model of Alexander disease
The path to Zanvastro began more than 30 years ago in Messing’s laboratory at the university’s School of Veterinary Medicine and Waisman Center. Working with Michael Brenner, now professor emeritus of neurobiology at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, Messing engineered mice to overexpress the gene that makes glial fibrillary acidic protein, or GFAP.
The mice developed protein clumps throughout their brains, concentrated in astrocytes, cells that help support nerve cells. These GFAP deposits, called Rosenthal fibers, are a classic feature of Alexander disease, giving the researchers an unexpected connection between their experiment and the human disorder.
“We had, really without intending to, created a mouse that produced these classic lesions of Alexander disease,” Messing says.
Rosenthal fibers (dark red), a hallmark of Alexander disease, appeared in these brain samples from a rodent model designed by UW–Madison researchers Albee Messing and Tracy Hagemann. Credit: Messing and Hagemann
Genetic analysis of people with Alexander disease confirmed that mutations in the GFAP gene were the root cause, a discovery Messing and Brenner made in the late 1990s. Identifying those mutations allowed doctors to diagnose the disease through blood tests instead of invasive brain biopsies. It also pointed the researchers toward a treatment that could reduce the protein’s harmful accumulation.
“This provided an obvious and specific strategy for therapy — the GFAP protein,” Messing explains.
Reducing GFAP buildup at its source
To test that approach, Messing and Tracy Hagemann, an associate research professor at the Waisman Center, developed improved rodent models of Alexander disease. Their search focused on finding a drug that could lower GFAP levels, leading to a collaboration with Ionis to develop antisense oligonucleotides, or ASOs. These small pieces of DNA can suppress production of a targeted protein.
Zanvastro uses this approach to reduce GFAP production before the protein can accumulate and cause further damage. Positive results from ASO treatment in rodents led to the human trial and, ultimately, the approval of the first and only disease-modifying treatment for Alexander disease.
“The whole program of research would not have been possible without the support and participation from the patient and family community, to whom we will always be grateful,” Messing says.

title: NTU and Singfilm Solar send perovskite solar cells to space aboard CRIMSON-1 satellite
content:
NTU and Singfilm Solar send perovskite solar cells to space aboard CRIMSON-1 satellite
Nanyang Technological University (NTU Singapore) has launched CRIMSON-1, a nanosatellite carrying perovskite solar cells developed together with NUS spin-off
Singfilm Solar
, marking the first time a Singapore-made perovskite solar module has flown in orbit. The satellite lifted off on October 1 aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, and was deployed about 520 km above Earth using Exolaunch's EXOpod Nova system.
The team from NTU Satellite Research Centre and their partners. Image credit: NTU
CRIMSON-1 is NTU's 14th research satellite, built by the university's Satellite Research Centre (SaRC). The 5 kg, shoebox-sized spacecraft is designed to run a year-long mission testing two technologies under real orbital conditions: the perovskite solar cells, and an onboard AI system that filters and analyzes satellite imagery before transmitting it to Earth, cutting down on the raw data scientists would otherwise need to process manually.
The flexible perovskite module, built on ultrathin glass, is mounted alongside the satellite's primary gallium arsenide panels, which will continue to power the spacecraft itself. The mission will measure how well the perovskite cells withstand the physical stresses of launch and the subsequent radiation, thermal cycling and vacuum conditions of low Earth orbit, along with their actual power output once in space. Gallium arsenide cells, the current standard for spacecraft, cost between US$250 and US$450 per watt; perovskite cells are thinner, lighter and have the potential to be manufactured far more cheaply, which is the core appeal for future satellite designs.
"This mission marks the first spaceflight of a flexible perovskite solar module built on ultrathin glass, and the first deployment of a Singapore-made solar module in orbit," said Hou Yi, Assistant Professor at NUS and founder of Singfilm Solar. NTU Deputy President Professor Christian Wolfrum added that "CRIMSON-1 carries next-generation perovskite solar cells and edge AI computing into orbit. These technologies can only be validated under real space conditions."
CRIMSON-1 is backed by Singapore's National Space Agency (NSAS) under its Space Access Programme, part of the national Space Technology Development Programme, which has allocated S$210 million (about US$157 million) to space technology R&D since 2022. The Infocomm Media Development Authority secured the satellite's spectrum and orbital resources through the UN's International Telecommunication Union. "Perovskite solar cells will provide a compelling advantage over conventional panels - their thin, lightweight properties make them particularly well suited for space applications, where every gram matters," said Ngiam Le Na, NSAS's chief executive.
NTU has previously flown perovskite cells in space on its
ARCADE satellite in 2023
, as part of a
broader slate of space projects under Singapore's Space Technology Program
. Singfilm Solar, which spun out of NUS, reported a record 22.6% power conversion efficiency for a perovskite solar panel in 2024.

title: Prussian blue framework pushes perovskite solar cells to 26.9% efficiency, holds up in 30×30 cm submodules
content:
Prussian blue framework pushes perovskite solar cells to 26.9% efficiency, holds up in 30×30 cm submodules
Researchers at Xiamen University, Jinan University, Tsinghua University, Xi'an Jiaotong University, Uppsala University in Sweden, the Institute of High Energy Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the Shanghai Advanced Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and
Guangdong Mellow Energy
have developed a Prussian blue-based strategy to control both crystallization and ion migration in perovskite solar cells, achieving a champion efficiency of 26.9% in small-area cells that held up at scale in large submodules.
The team incorporated a lattice-matched Prussian blue scaffold into the perovskite film as a structural template. Using in situ grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) and X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) measurements at the Beijing and Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facilities, they found that the Prussian blue framework converts the film's typically uncontrolled, homogeneous nucleation into a more ordered, heterogeneous process. It suppressed the formation of non-photoactive δ-FAPbI₃ phases in favor of the photoactive α-FAPbI₃ phase, promoted crystal growth along a preferred orientation, and relieved tensile strain in the film. Separately, the framework's redox-active Fe–C≡N–Fe network helped convert lead⁰ and iodine⁰ defects, while its rigid, open cage structure locked mobile cations in place, suppressing the ion migration that normally degrades perovskite devices under operation.
The strategy yielded champion power conversion efficiencies of 26.1% in n-i-p architecture and 26.9% in p-i-n architecture (26.2% certified) for small-area cells. Scaling up, the team reached 23.4% in 6×6 cm minimodules and a certified 22.9% in 30×30 cm submodules. Submodules with initial efficiencies of 20.2–21.0% showed no discernible decline relative to a silicon reference cell over five months of outdoor testing, alongside robust performance under accelerated aging.

title: Who Had Power At That Trump AI Summit?
content: • The Big Read: Why a legal blitz over AI hacks is inevitable • Sean Parker’s quiet resurrection job • Plus, Recommendations—our weekly pop culture picks: “ The Permanent Questions ,” “ This Cursed Beautiful Land ” and “ East of Eden ” The AI titans probably all fly private. But if any of them did travel commercial regularly, they’d’ve long ago earned top-tier, drink-the-champagne-dry status just via their frequent cross-country jaunts to Washington. There they were again on Tuesday, convening at the White House for another powwow on AI safety and data-center construction. The result of those conversations was the unveiling of a new voluntary pledge signed by the moguls to police themselves. Trump called it a “morally binding” agreement. It could also be seen as an effort akin to allowing the sugar-addled denizens of a schoolyard recess to manage themselves. At one point during the summit, Trump and the AI leaders went outside to take questions from the media. That worsted-wool group included Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman and many others. Among them, I could count men who are enemies, frenemies, allies, business partners and sworn-to-the-death rivals. And in this crowd, none of those labels are mutually exclusive. Seldom does such a group get together in full public view, and clips from the press conference went viral, with internet detectives scrutinizing the interactions between the billionaires and their appearances—hoping to sleuth out who seemed the happiest, uneasiest and most powerful. It reminded me of a popular parlor game in Britain where people try to divine the true nature of the relationships among the royals whenever those bald pates gather around a Buckingham Palace balcony. What fun! So I decided to call in an expert: Abbie Maroño, a British-born behavioral scientist and an authority on body language who has consulted for the likes of the FBI, the Secret Service and Interpol. My conversation with her, which has been edited and condensed, appears below. Dario Amodei got perhaps the most speaking time, so let’s start there. What could you tell about him from how he acted? He was animated, and he used a lot of gestures where he was talking with his hands. He showed a lot of behaviors that coincide with what we could think of as confidence. However, what’s so interesting with him is that his entire aura very much leaks discomfort. He oozes anxiety while trying to show the behaviors of confidence. Using big gestures where everything’s over the top—that’s not actually what confidence looks like. Confidence is smooth. All of those gestures were done so fast. It’s like he’s in his head thinking: “Use your hands, use your hands—show confidence.” And when he does have seconds of pause, he holds his hands together and grips them. Those are self-soothing displays that we do when we’re trying to calm down. What about Mark Zuckerberg, who stood next to Trump for much of the time? Mark actually emanated power. He stood next to a huge source of power—Trump—and he was comfortable. What’s really interesting is, as he steps forward toward Trump, Trump steps back and turns toward him. It’s a dance between them that communicates an unwritten agreement—that Mark does have power. And Trump very much respects people with power. Zuckerberg never acts over the top. He’s not the biggest expresser there. His voice is very grounded. He looks around enough. He’s not looking down. He’s not, you know, darting his eyes everywhere. And there’s, like, a sense that he’s in total agreement with Trump. Everything he’s saying, Trump is nodding along in complete agreement. Did you notice Elon Musk sorta off in the background there? Yeah, he spends most of the time with his arms crossed and moves around considerably less than everyone else. Sometimes people read crossed arms as a defensive gesture, but crossing your arms is a default human position. What I get from him is that he’s quite socially detached and observational. He watches what happens. He doesn’t really speak that often. He doesn’t turn toward Trump the way that Zuckerberg does when Trump is speaking, and I think that really shows that rocky nature between Elon and Trump. When a figure of authority is speaking, you orientate toward them. That’s how you show respect. I don’t think he’s being disrespectful , but he isn’t showing as much respect as the others. Anything else stand out to you? Trump’s introduction to Amodei was quite interesting. He calls him forward and says, “Whatever he says is OK.” I think that’s Trump saying, “You’re here because I’m allowing it” without explicitly saying it. Huh. I didn’t get the same sense from Trump’s comment. It was to kind of remind Amodei that he holds the power there—that Amodei’s words are OK only because he, Trump, says they’re OK. It’s Trump’s reminder to Amodei that “if you’re in with me, you’re in with the cool kids—you’re good. But, you know, don’t overstep the mark.” —Abram Brown ( abe@theinformation.com ) Weekend’s Latest Stories The Big Read AI Agents Are Going Rogue. Novel Legal Battles Are Next Most existing laws weren’t written with AI in mind. But Silicon Valley is bracing itself for a wave of legal action over AI hacks. Sean Parker Spreads the Gospel of AI Music Two years ago, a Sean Parker–led investing group took command of Stability AI, a onetime darling of AI images. With the backing of the major record labels, Stability now hopes to convince musicians to fully embrace a technology that has unnerved parts of entertainment. Listening: “ The Permanent Questions ” The philosophizing of David Brooks, the longtime center-right pundit, is something like a box of Junior Mints: a not unpleasant, old-timey flavor that has definitely fallen out of favor these days. But when most new podcasts have all the substance of, say, a stale pouch of Big League Chew, Brooks’ “The Permanent Questions” is an inviting alternative. Brooks spent several decades opining on society, culture, faith and politics as a New York Times op-ed columnist—he departed last January. “The Permanent Questions” is his debut at his new full-time home, The Atlantic. With the series, he puts aside his interest in Washington’s hurly-burly and trains his attention on longer-standing, more existential matters, like what constitutes a good life, humanity’s place in the cosmos and the meaning of transcendentalist mysticism. Those topics might seem too weighty for amiable chitchat, but Brooks does a pleasant job of unpacking them with his guests, who’ve so far included University of Notre Dame philosopher Meghan Sullivan and Pulitzer Prize–winning author Ayad Akhtar. Their chats are far-reaching—one got me to finally realize what has been bothering me so much about a friendship that has gone cold. And as they go, they bring up any number of other thinkers and wellsprings of inspiration. Plato and Aristotle get mentioned a lot. So does C.S. Lewis. I enjoyed how one conversation even wound its way around to A Tribe Called Quest, the formative 1990s hip-hop group. In other words: Can Brooks and his company kick it? With a touch of arthritis, yes, they can. —Abram Brown Reading: “ This Cursed Beautiful Land ” by Evan Gershkovich In 2017, Evan Gershkovich, the American-born son of Russian immigrants, was a peon at The New York Times: a news assistant, a clerk-type job that provided very little opportunity to do any actual reporting. “I was a bystander to the real business of newsgathering,” he recalls in “This Cursed Beautiful Land.” “I watched as world-altering events splashed over the front page, one after the other.” Gershkovich wanted to get closer to the action. Gosh, did he ever. After upending his life and moving to Moscow, he worked first at The Moscow Times and later at The Wall Street Journal. By 2023, his reporting had drawn the attention of the FSB—the successor to the Soviet KGB—and in an incident that made global headlines at the time, Gershkovich was arrested and imprisoned, accused of spying for America. (He wasn’t, he says—and acknowledges that he would’ve made a terrible spook.) More than a year later, Gershkovich was released in a prisoner swap between America and Russia. “This Cursed Beautiful Land,” a reference to the Russia he discovered as a reporter and the one he came to understand from within a “tiny concrete box” at Lefortovo prison, is Gershkovich’s attempt to wrap his mind around everything that happened to him and the brutal horror of his family’s homeland. It is part espionage thriller—masked agents grabbed him at a steakhouse, threw a hood over his head, then subjected him to days of interrogation broken up by soft rock music—and part jailhouse memoir. At Lefortovo, Gershkovich struck up a friendship with his cellmate, Sergei, who helped him learn the ropes: Always wipe your shoes before entering a cell, turn on the tap before using the toilet, never offer to shake hands. As Gershkovich adjusts, a Russian idiom, which roughly translates as “You’re not Russian if you haven’t sat in prison,” begins to carry more weight in his mind. —A.B. Watching: “ East of Eden ” Netflix hasn’t shown much interest lately in the prestige-iest end of television, contenting itself instead with what its executives internally have referred to as “gourmet cheeseburgers”—shows like “The Diplomat,” “Wednesday” and “The Night Agent.” Perhaps “East of Eden,” a new adaptation of John Steinbeck’s 1952 lengthy meditation on evil and good, is a signal that it is changing direction—or that it certainly can change direction: The series, a visually lush and superbly acted affair, is a masterful adaptation. Over seven episodes, Netflix’s “East of Eden” goes full, glorious sprawl with Steinbeck’s saga, treating it with deft felicity. Like the novel, the series spans more than a half-century, beginning with a bloodied, battered Cathy (Florence Pugh) crawling onto the farmhouse porch belonging to the Trask brothers, Adam (Christopher Abbott) and Charles (Mike Faist), in late-19th-century Connecticut. Flashbacks follow to the siblings’ troubled, violent relationship with their father (Tracy Letts) and Cathy’s past, which, by comparison, makes the Trask boys’ upbringing look like a cheery NBC sitcom. Tenderhearted Adam falls in love with Cathy, and they set out for California; Charles stays behind, a misery. Still, the Golden State is not quite the promised land Adam envisioned, especially after Cathy abandons him, leaving Adam to raise their infant sons, Cal and Aron. The greatest performance might belong to Korean American actor Hoon Lee, who appears as Lee, a servant hired by Adam who becomes his children’s chief caregiver. That makes him an emotional ballast for a tale full of family melodrama and several generations of neglect—enough woe, of course, to make it seem like a higher power has cursed the various Trask siblings to resemble the Biblical characters of Cain and Abel. The most significant update to Steinbeck’s story is showrunner Zoe Kazan’s treatment of Cathy, who becomes a bordello madam: Steinbeck depicted her as a monster. Kazan seeks greater nuance without ever falling into the trap of trying to make her oversympathetic. Kazan herself faces a formidable family legacy. She is the granddaughter of filmmaker Elia Kazan, who also tried his hand at adapting “East of Eden” in 1955, a ham-fisted version that narrowed its focus to the novel’s final chapters. Zoe’s success with “East of Eden”—so much for family curses, eh?—should raise expectations among the Packy McCormick set for her next Netflix project: an adaptation of another epic, Larry McMurtry’s “Lonesome Dove.” —A.B.

title: AI Agents Are Going Rogue. Novel Legal Battles Are Next
content: Once just an element of science fiction, revelations of AIs gone rogue are increasingly everyday occurrences. As a result, Silicon Valley founders and executives are girding themselves for what they see as the inevitable: a cascade of legal action. One of those people is Paul Grewal, chief legal and global affairs officer at Cognition, a top AI startup building coding agents. He thinks criminal cases will face long odds, but he can picture opportunistic prosecutors taking a shot at the developers behind rogue agents, emboldened by growing public sentiment that AI companies are acting recklessly. “You’ve got a huge percentage of the regular public at least aware of what’s going on,” he said. “So I could imagine—in a certain political climate—that temptation for ambitious prosecutors will still be there.” Or, as Joel Thayer, president of the Digital Progress Institute, a tech policy think tank, put it: “All these AI companies are going to get sued up the wazoo.” Whether any of those legal battles will actually prevail in court is another question entirely. Until the summer, concern about AIs committing potentially illegal acts on their own was a matter of hypotheticals. Then in July, OpenAI admitted that swarms of its autonomous AI agents had broken out of a training environment and hacked Hugging Face, a repository of open-source models. Since then, OpenAI has been implicated in a series of similar attacks, including one against RubyGems, a nonprofit programming website, and several intrusions into Australian and U.S. government websites. Anthropic , Google and other AI giants have also disclosed rogue AI incidents, though none as serious as the Hugging Face hack, which involved hundreds of agents. One AI hacking lawsuit has already been filed, the first such action in the wake of the recent wave of AI hacking incidents. The plaintiff in the suit—a New York–based public interest law group, Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology—isn’t the most obvious candidate to go after an AI company. In its suit, filed earlier this week in California, the firm used an esoteric legal argument to say that OpenAI’s hacking of Hugging Face caused it harm. Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue has said his startup doesn’t have the resources or “the will” to pursue legal action against OpenAI. (Getty Images) As AI has pushed all sorts of fields into new frontiers, these lawsuits will likely do the same to the U.S. legal system. Any lawyer helming legal action against a company whose AI has broken bad will have to take a novel approach for a simple reason: Very little state or federal regulation has been written specifically around AI. There’s really just one piece of benchmark federal legislation governing hacks, the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, which dates back to 1986. That law revolves around the idea of intent—that hackers act with a premeditated intention to damage or steal from a company. Obviously, the creators of that law didn’t consider a time when a hack could be orchestrated by something that wasn’t a living, breathing person. Nor did they consider whether the makers of an AI could be held liable for their creations’ decision to spontaneously—and independently—commit an act that would be a felony if carried out by flesh-and-blood people. This week, lawmakers took steps to bring that law into the AI age. On Thursday, Sens. Josh Hawley and Chris Murphy announced legislation that would update the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and make it easier for legal cases against AI companies to be filed. In the current landscape, though, Bahrad Sokhansanj, a senior research scholar at the Institute for Law and AI, thinks it would be a stretch to successfully apply current state and federal laws to the developers of rogue AI agents—at least for the incidents that have so far occurred. “It’d be very hard to see how they could be held liable based on what we understand now,” he said. AI liability battles could take many different forms. The most obvious one would involve the victim of an AI hack suing the company that created the AI in civil court. Still, in the most prominent AI hack so far, the victim, Hugging Face, hasn’t yet pursued legal action. Shortly after the hack’s disclosure, Hugging Face CEO and co-founder Clement Delangue said that his 200-person startup didn’t “necessarily have the legal resources or the will” for such a lawsuit and instead called for OpenAI to commit $100 million in compute resources to help Hugging Face build cyberdefenses. But what would’ve happened if Hugging Face had decided to sue OpenAI? The startup would have had a difficult time demonstrating clear damages—whether monetary or reputational, said Sokhansanj. Indeed, Hugging Face’s fortunes have only improved since it was hacked. In September, Nvidia announced it was acquiring the company for nearly $13 billion. A few weeks later, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang joked on a New York Times podcast that he “probably had to pay a lot more” for the company after the hacking incident made it a household name. In the same conversation, Huang was asked whether he would have sued OpenAI if Nvidia had owned Hugging Face at the time of the hack. “Obviously, if damage was done to our company, we would have to consider all options,” Huang replied. An Nvidia spokesperson declined to comment on whether Nvidia is considering any legal action against OpenAI. OpenAI and Nvidia remain close business partners . Sen. Josh Hawley has proposed legislation that would update key federal legislation that could make it easier for legal action to be brought against AI developers. (Getty Images) That interwoven relationship is one of the reasons Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology decided to file its own lawsuit this week against OpenAI over the Hugging Face incident. “The structure of the industry is such that organizations and individuals that are harmed are not necessarily incentivized to do this on their own behalf,” said Tyler Whitmer, the organization’s founder and CEO. But what on earth, some will ask, does Whitmer’s group have to do with the Hugging Face incident? A California Supreme Court ruling from a few years ago established that organizations suing in the public interest could establish standing by arguing they had to divert resources from their existing missions to account for the issue they’re suing about. Whitmer’s organization is arguing that it had to set aside its prior work, such as filing public records requests and tracking AI safety incidents, to prepare briefings for regulators about the Hugging Face hack. The group’s decision to file its lawsuit in a California state court rather than a federal one comes with an advantage. In federal court, it would need to prove that OpenAI intentionally allowed its agents to hack Hugging Face. But the group hopes to prevail by taking advantage of a 1987 California statute that requires a plaintiff to show a defendant knowingly accessed computer systems without permission—a seemingly lower standard than the federal one, which requires proving intent. And there’s a new law passed by California last year that bans defendants from skirting responsibility by arguing that AI “autonomously” caused harm. Rep. Lori Trahan has co-sponsored a new bill that hopes to stop AIs from causing catastrophes before they happen. (Getty Images) Rather than asking for monetary damages, Whitmer hopes the court will force OpenAI to change its development practices. Nothing will get decided quickly. The case will take months at least to get through the California legal system, Whitmer acknowledged. Plausibly, it could even go for years. The issue of standing—who has the right to sue AI developers—will be a crucial factor in determining how many more cases surface. Presumably, other public interest groups could mount similar lawsuits. State or federal prosecutors could also take legal action against AI companies, and the arguments would vary based on the agencies bringing the action and whether they’re following civil or criminal routes. So far, a coalition of 15 state attorneys general has demanded that OpenAI preserve information related to the hack for potential litigation. None has brought a case so far, though that could change any day. As for the feds, the FTC recently opened a probe into OpenAI and Anthropic over the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers, though it remains unclear whether the investigation will focus on the issue of rogue agents. If the Justice Department decided to pursue a criminal case, it would likely have to center its arguments around the 1986 Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Still, its prosecutors might soon have greater opportunities to pursue legal action against AI companies. The legislation proposed by Hawley and Murphy to update that act would hold AI agent developers criminally and civilly liable for “knowing operation” of an AI agent that acts recklessly. Hawley and Murphy have yet to share the text of the bill, but it seems like it would lower the federal standard for culpability—so an AI company wouldn’t have needed to act with human-directed intent to be held liable. Other Congressional offices have proposed legislation that focuses on preventing rogue behavior from happening in the first place rather than punishing AI companies in a hack’s aftermath. The AI Incident Reporting Act, a bill proposed by Republican Congressman Nathaniel Moran, would allow the Justice Department to enforce penalties if companies don’t report critical safety incidents in a timely manner. Top Trump advisers like David Sacks, the former White House AI czar, have insisted that existing laws should be sufficient to prevent catastrophic events. Bill Gates highlighted the limits of current laws to stop AI companies from acting recklessly in a New York Times interview: “Say you kill 100 million people—you want to use a lawsuit? I almost can’t keep a straight face.” (YouTube: @ezrakleinshow) But as one Congressional staffer working on AI legislation pointed out, existing liability laws likely aren’t enough to dissuade companies from engaging in the type of activity that could cause such severe incidents. If rogue AI agents were to take down a major electrical grid during a heat wave, the ensuing legal action would likely bankrupt the agents’ developer, after all. In a podcast interview with The New York Times earlier this week, Bill Gates described the notion that product liability laws can adequately protect society from the worst-case AI scenarios—such as a bioweapons attack—as laughable. “Say you kill 100 million people—you want to use a lawsuit?” Gates said. “I almost can’t keep a straight face.” That’s why new regulations like the proposed Frontier Act could be so important. The legislation, an ambitious bipartisan effort from Reps. Lori Trahan and Jay Obernolte, seeks to establish preventative measures to stop rogue AI incidents from ever happening. It would require developers to create risk assessments and submit to third-party audits. The Frontier Act was created out of a worry that AI agents could bring catastrophic risks, which it defines as causing over 50 deaths or $1 billion in damage. Even if companies aren’t themselves victims of AI hacking, they could still feel some pain from such incidents. “One question I would have—and I don’t have an answer to it—is, ‘What happens to insurance?’” said Sokhansanj, the research scholar at the Institute for Law and AI. The idea of insurance as a preventative measure against rogue AI incidents gained prominence this week after the White House brought together top companies including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta Platforms to sign a voluntary joint agreement. Among other provisions, the accord laid out that each company would designate a committee from its board of directors to receive reports from third-party auditors. As investor Gavin Baker explained on X, those board members will now have a fiduciary duty to respond to the reports. If they don’t, they could be denied directors’ and officers’ liability insurance and open themselves up to legal vulnerability. A nearly two-year-old startup, the Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Co., is building insurance products for companies developing the agents and models that could someday go rogue. Run by Rune Kvist, a former Anthropic employee, the company earlier this year landed ElevenLabs, an AI voice startup, as its first AI insurance policy customer. Kvist said his startup is now fielding calls from major frontier labs that want to buy more comprehensive policies, which could cover incidents similar to the Hugging Face attack. Those policies would offer traditional insurance payouts. But Kvist said the insurance will be most attractive to AI labs because it will grant them an air of credibility: They’re engaging third-party insurance firms that are evaluating their systems and have a financial interest in making sure those labs are behaving themselves. Kvist is hopeful that the company can launch the policies by the end of the year. “Labs are seeing this as a tool for earning trust from the public,” he said.

title: OpenAI Hires Top Trump AI Official to Work on National Security
content: OpenAI is continuing to fill out its leadership bench with former Trump administration officials. Thomas Lind, who previously led AI policy at the Office of the National Cyber Director, joined OpenAI this week, an OpenAI spokesperson confirmed. ONCD is a key office within the White House that played a leading role in putting together a June executive order on AI. Lind will lead cyber and strategic risk on OpenAI’s national security policy team, which is led by Sasha Baker, the former deputy Under Secretary of Defense for Policy in the Biden administration. OpenAI and its executives have been stepping up efforts to strengthen the company’s ties to the Trump administration. In July, it hired Dean Ball, who previously worked in the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy and helped draft the administration’s July 2025 AI Action Plan . Last year, OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife Anna donated $25 million to Donald Trump’s super PAC. Lind’s hire comes at a critical juncture for AI regulation. Recent incidents involving rogue AI, including a swarm of OpenAI agents hacking into the open source repository Hugging Face, have led to calls for new laws from policymakers and safety groups. The Trump administration has resisted efforts to establish new regulation, though November’s midterm elections could bring further legislative and oversight efforts if the Democrats take control of either Congressional chamber. Lind’s former agency, ONCD, was at the center of the Trump administration’s efforts to wrangle AI policy. The office had been working on a cybersecurity-related executive order on AI before Anthropic announced its latest model Mythos last April, which the company did not release to the public because of safety concerns. The planned order evolved to deal with the new threats posed by cyber models, The Information previously reported . Formally signed by Trump in June after a tumultuous back-and-forth process between AI companies and different factions within the administration, the executive order established a voluntary framework for AI developers to submit their models for government review before releasing them to the public. The framework went into effect in early August, though it has been widely criticized for a lack of transparency after the White House declined to release it publicly, as well as continued uncertainty over whether it will include open-source model providers. As the White House continues to grapple with how much AI oversight it wants to perform, ONCD remains at the center of key decision-making around the framework’s implementation. That includes the framework’s trusted partner program , which establishes the organizations that get early access to advanced AI models after they go through government review. Lind left ONCD in June, according to his LinkedIn. He had joined the office in April 2025 as the senior director for intelligence, becoming the head of policy a year later. He previously worked as an intelligence officer in the National Security Agency. OpenAI continues to invest heavily in cyber efforts. In August, OpenAI’s Brockman released a blog post arguing that the Hugging Face incident was a “watershed moment” for cybersecurity. Later that month, the company led an open letter calling on organizations and governments to bolster their cyber defense efforts. In September, the company committed $1 billion for its “Daybreak for Frontline Defenders” initiative to subsidize access to its frontier models and provide technical assistance. “Tom is a key addition to our national security team, bringing expertise across AI policy, cybersecurity, and strategic risk,” OpenAI’s Baker said in a statement. “His hire reflects OpenAI’s continued investment in addressing the national security challenges of increasingly capable AI and ensuring this technology is used to benefit and protect the country. His expertise is even more important as AI becomes central to the national security agenda, with the Office of the National Cyber Director playing a growing role in shaping AI policy.”

title: Sean Parker Spreads the Gospel of AI Music
content: To the music industry, Sean Parker has been many things. As co-founder of Napster, he was first an “outlaw renegade,” as he himself puts it. After his time at Facebook, his next act was as an early Spotify investor—putting in money while at Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund—and as a longtime Spotify board member. Parker today hungers to be the guy who gets recording artists and music producers hooked on artificial intelligence. And he hopes to do so through the quiet resurrection of Stability AI, the once red-hot startup that nearly cratered out of existence before he took control of it two years ago. As Parker tells it, bringing change to the music world isn’t for the faint of heart. “Generally, you find that people who are very passionate about music go into the music industry, get burned and then maybe never come back,” he said, breaking a long-held silence on his hopes and plans for Stability. “I’m probably one of a very few people who is enough of a masochist.” Stability is something of an unlikely vehicle for Parker’s return to music. After the startup’s founding in 2020, it was initially best known for its image-generation model, Stable Diffusion, which got talked about in the same company as OpenAI’s Dall-E. It zoomed to a $1 billion valuation. But overspending and staff unrest led to founder and CEO Emad Mostaque’s ousting in 2024. In came Parker and a group of other investors, who shored up the perilous financial situation with an $80 million infusion—and renegotiated with the startup’s cloud providers to forgive several hundred million dollars of debt. In the process, Parker became Stability’s executive chair, while the CEO job went to Prem Akkaraju, former head of Weta Digital—the special effects company started by director Peter Jackson—and a longtime friend of Parker. Stability AI CEO Prem Akkaraju was previously head of Weta Digital, the special effects company founded by director Peter Jackson. He and Parker are longtime friends. (Getty Images) For a while, Stability seemed to disappear. A month or so ago, it rather unexpectedly rematerialized, saying it had raised $76 million in fresh funding, with a trio of prominent new investors: Sony Music, Warner Music Group and Universal Music Group, the three major record labels. (The startup is spending the funding on research, product development and compute; neither Parker nor Akkaraju would comment on the company’s new valuation.) With the money and investors, Parker and Akkaraju are now focusing the company on developing AI for music industry professionals. In addition to the investment, the labels have also cut licensing deals with Stability, which will use their catalogs to train its AI. Already over the last few months, Stability has released three new audio-generation models and AI music-editing software. Stability’s small and medium-size models are available for free for non-commercial use. Businesses with more than $1 million in revenue need to sign licensing deals to use any of the models. The AI can generate whole instrumental tracks and small snippets of audio through natural-language text prompts. An upcoming update will let users also direct the AI through audio of themselves humming a melody or beatboxing a drum pattern. “Natural language is a pretty bad bottleneck for describing music,” said Zach Evans, Stability’s head of audio research. “People tend to want to actually use music itself to describe music.” By focusing on AI for music professionals, Parker and Akkaraju are choosing to sidestep the crowded field of startups making AI music apps for everyday consumers, like Suno and Udio. (Those consumer apps generate both instruments and lyrics—Stability’s AI does not produce lyrics, as it assumes artists will want to keep control over that part of creating a song.) Still, those startups could refocus on the professional market. Meanwhile, Parker and Akkaraju are gambling that none of the big players in tech that have released their own AI music features—a list that includes OpenAI, Meta Platforms and Google—will choose to pay attention to their corner of the business and snuff it out. The stiffest existing rival to Stability’s AI is probably Google’s audio-generation model, Lyria. But unlike Lyria, Stability’s models are open weight, which allows their users to tweak and customize them. Stability’s AI also allows for greater editing within a song and can handle longer song lengths. When I spoke to Warner Music CEO Robert Kyncl, he readily acknowledged that the specter of competition looms over Stability. “What’s stopping a better-funded competitor from jumping in? Well, if you grew up on the internet, you know the answer is ‘Nothing,’” said Kyncl, who was previously YouTube’s chief business officer and an early key Netflix executive. “Like I always used to say when I was at Netflix or at YouTube: ‘We’re always paranoid, because our competition is just a click away and raising money from Andreessen Horowitz.’ That’s a way of life.” Parker maintains that Stability has moved as fast as possible in its comeback efforts. He felt the licensing deals and record label investments were essential to secure first if Stability hoped to win legitimacy with major customers: Those negotiations with the labels weren’t going to happen overnight, and he had no interest in returning to his renegade past. “With anything Hollywood related, it takes a little more time to do things the right way,” said Parker. “It’s a case of a lesson learned from when I was first starting out: Asking for forgiveness rather than permission is generally not the right strategy.” The turnaround efforts at Stability AI represent the latest attempt by Sean Parker—the Napster co-founder and early Spotify investor—to disrupt the music world. (Getty Images) Kyncl said his decision to partner with Stability was a bet on Parker’s past at Spotify and “passion for solving issues within the music industry,” as he politely put it—as well as his yearslong relationship with Akkaraju, who led the talks with Warner. (Akkaraju and Kyncl originally met at a Cannes Film Festival party in 2014.) More fundamentally, Kyncl was also concerned about the idea of Warner sitting out the AI era. “I don’t want the lessons of the file-sharing era to go by the wayside,” he said. (Warner has also done licensing deals with Suno and Udio.) As Akkaraju and Parker talk up Stability’s tools in the entertainment world, they find themselves in a landscape where the perception around AI seems to be shifting. The media and entertainment elite initially met the AI boom with a sense of dread—and waves of copyright litigation. Some of those legal battles continue. Universal Music and Sony Music, for instance, are still suing Suno over copyright infringement. (Warner Music has settled with Suno.) And The New York Times Co. and other publishers remain locked in a fight with OpenAI. Yet there are some signs that entertainment is beginning to warm to AI. In March, actor Ben Affleck sold his AI startup, which has been working on movie-editing software, to Netflix for $587 million. Three months later, Google said it would invest $75 million in A24—the much-loved indie studio with a shelf of Oscar gold—and partner with it to develop AI tools. Akkaraju tries to take every opportunity he can to coax the AI reticent to try Stability’s products. At a recent party for his child’s school at his Los Angeles home, Akkaraju dragged a music supervisor from one of the major studios away from the festivities and into his study to give the software a test spin. How’d it go? “It was probably the same reaction as when a mailman saw email for the first time,” Akkaraju said. “He was super excited.” When I asked Akkaraju about the tall challenges I can picture lying ahead for Stability, he had a succinct reply. “If I wanted to do easier stuff,” he said, “I would just sell crunchy, salty snacks.” For his part, Parker sees nothing but fertile ground ahead. “The widespread use of AI tools and technologies for the creative class is, relatively speaking, in its infancy,” he said. “Ultimately, there’s a very big opportunity to augment the creative power of professional musicians who actually want to use these tools in a very creative, expressive way.”

title: AI Data Center Debt Is Showing Up Everywhere
content: Debt financing for data centers and related infrastructure has grown rapidly enough that it’s become its own category these days—credit analysts are breaking out AI versus non–AI-linked debt across markets to analyze new issuance and performance. Several asset managers in recent months have filed to create exchange-traded funds focused on AI or AI infrastructure–related debt. And right now, parts of this category aren’t doing so hot. In case you missed it, our own Dakin Campbell did a deep dive earlier this week on the cracks showing up in various financing markets fueling the AI build-out. There’s a lot going on, from wider spreads on tech giants’ corporate debt in the investment-grade market; to investors demanding bigger concessions in recent bonds for AI data center projects in the high-yield market; to skittishness in the bank loan market for AI project financing. Investors are getting choosier and taking a harder look at project-specific construction and other risks. Zeroing in on the high-yield market in particular, there’s a group of bonds that anyone with an interest in the AI build-out should be keeping an eye on. Overall, there have been at least 20 high-yield bond deals financing data center projects over the past 12 months, according to The Information’s story this week. The companies behind these projects, such as CleanSpark or TeraWulf, are hardly household names, and the project debt is often issued through even more obscure special purpose entities. But if you do a little digging, many of the biggest names in AI show up connected to these data center projects in some form, as direct tenants, customers of the tenants or providing some kind of credit support to get the financing done. That means markets for lower-rated issuers are financing at least some of the infrastructure supporting the biggest AI companies. (These deals generally finance the data center buildings and related infrastructure; they typically don’t finance the chips that go inside the data centers.) For instance, multiple project deals over the past year are for data centers leased to CoreWeave, which in turn counts Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI among its customers. One CoreWeave-related project financing is for two data centers where CoreWeave leases one and Alibaba Cloud leases the other. And that’s a more obvious connection than some of the rest. Several project financings are for space leased by AI infrastructure startup Fluidstack, with Google backing certain Fluidstack lease obligations. Fluidstack has been building and securing data centers for Anthropic, among others. Anthropic, meanwhile, has been dramatically expanding its use of Google’s TPU chips. Then there are two Nevada bond financings issued through special purpose entities, SV RNO Property Owner 1 LLC and PR RNO Property Owner 1 LLC. Fleet Data Centers, a portfolio company of asset manager Tract Capital, is developing both projects. Credit ratings reports for both described long-term leases to an unnamed investment-grade tenant—a May report noted the anonymous tenant had a more than $3 trillion market cap—which Bloomberg has previously reported is Nvidia in both cases. Nvidia has been increasingly securing data center capacity itself, both for its own use and to help customers secure capacity. Nvidia disclosed in August that it had $25 billion of not-yet-commenced data center lease commitments, mostly for its own use like product design and testing, and another $20 billion of future data center lease commitments that it plans to reassign to third parties. There’ve also been bond deals tied to data centers leased by Amazon and Oracle. And one for SB Energy’s Cosmos campus in Texas, where a SoftBank Group affiliate guarantees the tenant’s obligations under the lease, SB Energy’s initial public offering paperwork shows. As Dakin reported earlier this week, one of the most recent project bonds was a financing for a CleanSpark project for Meta. While there are some proposed dedicated funds for AI-related debt, many of these project financings have already worked their way into broader funds. That makes sense, as data center project debt itself has had a growing presence in the overall high-yield market. For instance, high-yield bond exchange-traded funds from asset managers including State Street and Charles Schwab count debt tied to Fluidstack-leased data centers and one of Fleet’s Nevada projects among their top holdings. To be sure, those are small slices—less than 1% each—of the overall ETFs, which hold debt across a wide range of sectors. In other words, even though it has become its own category in some ways, the AI debt boom has become tougher to avoid in general. Either way, it’s worth paying attention to who’s doing these financings and whom the data center capacity is really for—and how the next deals coming to market fare. 中核华兴自主研发“造岛机”在徐圩项目完成首次顶升
近日，由中核华兴承建、自主研发的江苏徐圩核能供热发电厂1号机组安全壳施工集成平台(简称“造岛机”)顺利完成首次顶升，正式从安装调试转入自主爬升阶段。该平台集自爬升、封闭作业与智能监控于一体，创新采用轻量化模块设计，集成平台系统、附墙支承、液压爬升、安全监控及折叠臂吊机等装备，有效降低研发成本并提升安拆效率。
“造岛机”具备三大核心功能：一是液压系统驱动机位同步顶升，不再依赖塔吊反复吊运模板挂架;二是顶部平台兼作堆场，折叠臂吊机在筒体周边完成钢筋、模板及预埋件转运，环轨吊服务壳间二次钢结构施工，减少人工倒运;三是全封闭作业层配合实时监控，为人员提供安全可靠的作业环境。项目部在顶升前开展了多轮堆载、同步爬升和附着承载试验，确保关键部位应力远低于安全限值，液压同步升降相邻机位高低差控制在毫米级，并具备超载与不同步自动报警停机功能。
平台完全投用后，安全壳内外壳可分层同步流水作业，环廊钢结构提前约6.8个月具备施工条件，周边厂房环形区制约提前约4.5个月解除;顶部平台随筒体爬升新增约520平方米材料堆场，6台折叠臂吊机可释放单台机组约15%至20%的塔吊运力，壳间环轨吊减少人工倒运约20%;全封闭作业层单台机组可减少高危吊装约1900次。
该装备的创新应用为核岛批量化、高质量建设提供了重大工程支撑，是中核华兴落实中核集团数字化、智能化转型要求的具体实践。中核华兴表示，将以装备换人力、以数据提工效、以体系保安全，把徐圩经验沉淀为可复制的“华兴方案”，持续推动核电工程更安全、更智能、更高效建设。

北大医院核医学科获EARL Theranostics Advanced-L2认证，诊疗一体化接轨国际标准
2026-10-03 16:22 北京大学第一医院 EARL认证 PET/CT 靶向治疗
北京大学第一医院核医学科近日正式获得由欧洲核医学会下属机构EARL(EANM Research Ltd.)颁发的Theranostics Advanced-L2认证，成为国内少数获此高级别认证的核医学诊疗一体化中心。该认证审核标准严苛，涵盖PET/CT定量准确性、治疗中心运营、患者安全管理及临床能力等综合维度，通过认证意味着科室的定量成像和靶向治疗数据达到国际互认标准，可与欧美先进核医学中心实现高水平接轨。
在认证评审期间，EANM候任主席Felix M. Mottaghy教授及Iva Hristova女士到访北大医院核医学科开展现场核查与交流，深入了解科室临床诊疗流程、质量管理体系及日常规范化运行情况，并围绕质量控制、技术规范及诊疗一体化建设等内容进行研讨。同期，意大利Vita-Salute大学全职教授、米兰San Raffaele研究所核医学系主任Arturo Chiti教授也到访科室，围绕人工智能、多模态影像及前沿技术在肺癌早期发现与精准表征中的应用作专题学术报告，分享国际前沿进展。
北大医院核医学科创建于1958年，是我国首批建立的核医学科之一，现为教育部"核技术应用"重点学科、国家新药临床试验机构核医学专业基地，在核素显像、脏器功能测定、核素治疗及放射性药物转化等领域具备深厚积累。此次获得EARL Theranostics Advanced-L2认证，将助力科室在肿瘤、心血管、神经系统等重大疾病领域进一步推动诊疗一体化体系建设，为患者提供精准、规范、国际水准的核医学诊疗服务。

博思得角箍缩磁体脉冲电源交付，X射线高压电源厂商正式入局核聚变装备
2026-10-03 17:05 博思得 TP电源 角箍缩磁体脉冲电源 可控核聚变
近日，博思得自主研发的角箍缩磁体脉冲电源(TP电源)完成交付，标志着这家X射线高压电源厂商正式切入可控核聚变赛道。该电源核心服务于角箍缩、场反位形FRC、磁化等离子体生成与磁约束压缩等实验，是磁约束可控核聚变与高能量密度物理研究的关键特种动力装备，具备纳秒级多阶段多路脉冲时序协同、超大电流强电磁干扰下波形保真、互感耦合多波形衰减精准调控等硬核性能，可匹配前沿聚变实验严苛工况。
博思得成立于2015年，专注于特种高压电源、脉冲功率电源、X光射线源及高压发生器等产品，下游覆盖医疗影像、工业检测、半导体与高端仪器三大领域。公司目前已申请发明专利近150项，获授权近80项，牵头完成国家发改委核心技术攻关专项，获评国家高新技术企业及国家专精特新"重点小巨人"企业。基于对角落缩磁体脉冲电源及可控核聚变产业的战略投入，博思得已设立全资子公司合肥博思聚能科技有限公司，聚焦聚变特种电源研发与产业化。
此类脉冲功率电源除支撑可控核聚变基础研究外，还可广泛适配脉冲强磁场构建、电磁驱动实验、特种等离子体加载及高能物理精密测试等高端科研场景，为高校与科研院所的前沿能源物理研究提供动力核心。博思得以"为生命注能，助工业强基"为使命，在上海、无锡、合肥设有生产研发中心，业务覆盖北美、南美、欧洲、亚洲、非洲等多个地区。此次TP电源交付，为国内聚变科研装备国产化迭代注入新动力。

华龙一号首台备用应急柴油机在三澳核电二号机组正式可用
10月2日，“华龙一号”首台备用应急柴油机(9LHW)在三澳核电二号机组完成替代并网试验，正式可用。该设备可顶替一、二期工程原有12台应急柴油发电机(EDG)中的任意一台，显著提升了电厂应急电源的冗余度、可靠性和检修灵活性。
三澳核电一期、二期各设3列应急母线，每列配置一台EDG，但因负荷无交叉供电，原有机组预防性检修窗口集中，影响大修工期。自2021年起，苍南核电推动新增备用柴油机项目，从设计源头改进，新建备用应急柴油发电机厂房(BDD)，并建设接入各机组的廊道与电缆，以解决可用率及运维经济性问题。
调试期间，苍南核电与中广核工程苍南项目部组建联合攻坚队，攻克滑油过滤器卡涩、回油管振动等难题，顺利完成24小时满负荷运转及替代试验。该项目填补了中国广核集团“华龙一号”新型备用柴油机自主调试技术空白，将重大设计变更转化为可靠安全屏障，为机组安全投运筑牢基础。

18国专家共商俄罗斯MBIR快堆国际研究中心科研规划：聚焦闭合燃料循环与大科学工程协同
在乌兹别克斯坦科学院核物理研究所(Institute of Nuclear Physics of the Academy of Sciences of the Republic of Uzbekistan, INP AS RUz)，基于多用途快速中子研究堆(Multi-purpose Fast Neutron Research Reactor, MBIR)建立的国际研究中心(International Research Center, IRC MBIR)咨询委员会第三次会议正式召开。本次会议吸引了来自俄罗斯、韩国、印度、独联体、巴西及非洲等18个国家的72家科研机构、高校与工业企业的150余名专家代表参会，共同商讨该重大科研基础设施的应用研究议程。
俄罗斯科学院(Russian Academy of Sciences, RAS)副院长、咨询委员会主席斯捷潘·卡尔梅科夫(Stepan Kalmykov)在开幕致辞中指出，MBIR快堆作为全球大科学(Mega-Science)装置版图的核心组成部分，对推进闭合核燃料循环(Closed Nuclear Fuel Cycle, CNFC)、放射性废物(Radioactive Waste, RAW)最小化处理以及拓宽全球裂变核能资源基础具有决定性意义。卡尔梅科夫强调，核科技创新是推动多学科协同发展的引擎，跨国学术界与工业界的多边对话有助于奠定未来数十年全球先进堆发展标准。
俄罗斯国家原子能公司(Rosatom)科学与战略副总监叶夫根尼·阿巴库莫夫(Evgeny Abakumov)表示，咨询委员会在塔什干举办，印证了MBIR已由区域性重点工程演进为汇聚全球前沿核物理思想的国际引力场。乌兹别克斯坦科学院院长沙夫卡特·阿尤波夫(Shavkat Ayupov)与核物理研究所所长伊尔哈姆·萨迪科夫(Ilkham Sadykov)亦指出，MBIR工程与乌兹别克斯坦升级后的VVR-SM研究堆及回旋加速器集群具有天然互补性，双方在耐辐照材料试验、数值计算程序对标验证及医用放射性同位素生产等应用科学领域具备广阔合作空间。
库尔恰托夫研究所(Kurchatov Institute)国家研究中心主任米哈伊尔·科瓦尔丘克(Mikhail Kovalchuk)通过书面致辞指出，MBIR快中子研究堆与现役PIK高通量稳态热中子反应堆构成了覆盖全能谱中子通量的大科学科研矩阵，是确保技术自主与催生突破性技术的关键基石。他倡议构建统一的科研纲要，并号召独联体各成员国深度融入相关科学合作。
IRC MBIR财团首席执行官瓦西里·康斯坦丁诺夫(Vasily Konstantinov)介绍了设施平台的新愿景。他提出，依托MBIR的工程设计方案，未来有望衍生开发小型模块化核动力装置(Small Modular Reactor, SMR);鉴于MBIR产生的大部分热能将用于转化为约50兆瓦的电能输出，该堆型本身即可作为未来先进快堆工程的示范平台。此外，项目还将全流程引入人工智能算法，赋能从堆芯辐照方案设计到试验结果分析的各项环节。
MBIR是一座热功率达150兆瓦(Megawatt Thermal, MWt)的钠冷快中子多用途研究堆(Sodium-Cooled Fast Reactor, SFR)，坐落于俄罗斯季米特洛夫格勒的俄罗斯核反应堆研究所(Research Institute of Atomic Reactors, NIIAR)园区，属于俄罗斯“先进核能与能源技术”国家科技专项的核心工程。工程目前正全面推进一回路主工艺安装：继2025年完成事故余热排出系统冷过滤器-捕集器定位、一回路热管道与压力容器接管嘴焊接、主钠库设备就位后，2026年两台单重达7.3吨、高5米、直径1.5米的事故工况热交换器已成功吊装就位，为加速第四代核能系统(Generation IV Nuclear Energy Systems)与双组分核能系统的研发铺平道路。

美国Valar Atomics拟在犹他州部署456座气冷核反应堆：打造9.6吉瓦超算数据中心专属供电系统
美国能源初创企业Valar Atomics正式提交了一项名为“蜂巢工程”(Project Beehive)的超大规模工业园区建设提案。该项目拟选址于美国犹他州普赖斯(Price, Utah)附近的联邦及州属土地，占地面积约9000英亩。整个工程规划集群式部署456座小型气冷核反应堆(Gas-Cooled Nuclear Reactors)，预计总装机发电容量将达到惊人的9.6吉瓦(Gigawatt, GW)，这一规模已超过目前犹他州全网平均4吉瓦发电负荷的两倍以上，接近其夏季近10吉瓦的用电峰值。
该项超密集核能综合体旨在从根本上破解人工智能(Artificial Intelligence, AI)算力中心面临的严峻用电瓶颈。随着前沿AI大模型训练与推理任务的爆发式增长，算力基础设施的用电需求已逼近传统区域电网的输配电极限，现有公共电网无法持续提供稳定、零碳且不受外界波动的专用基荷电力。为此，蜂巢工程将采用“核能直供电”模式，为超算中心构筑脱离电网脆弱性的闭环能源体系。
在土地使用审批层面，犹他州信托土地管理局(Utah School and Institutional Trust Lands Administration, SITLA)已于9月17日全票通过决议，正式批准为该项目租赁首期640英亩的信托土地。目前，其余联邦土地使用权正交由美国内政部土地管理局(Bureau of Land Management, BLM)进行合规性审议。
在反应堆工程架构与堆芯设计上，蜂巢工程放弃了传统轻水堆方案，全面转向采用高纯度氦气(Helium)作为主冷却剂的循环系统。这一设计显著规避了庞大的冷却水消耗，对于地处干旱缺水的美国西部高地尤为关键。此外，园区规划实现高度的核产业链自持，计划在封闭厂区内完成特种燃料元件的就地组装以及乏燃料(Spent Nuclear Fuel)的长期安全暂存。
该型反应堆选用了具备优异固有安全特性的三层各向同性包覆颗粒燃料(Tri-structural Isotropic Particle Fuel, TRISO)。燃料核芯外包裹有多层耐高温热解碳及碳化硅陶瓷保护壳，即便在遭遇全厂断电及极端高温恶劣工况下，燃料结构也不会熔毁，能够依靠物理材料特性自发阻止放射性裂变产物外泄。此前，Valar Atomics已在犹他州沙漠对其微堆核心原型——Ward 250微反应堆(Ward 250 Microreactor)进行了功能验证，并成功使用其所发电力驱动英伟达(Nvidia)计算设备平稳运行。

俄罗斯库尔恰托夫研究所将获57亿卢布财政预算支持：聚焦受控热核聚变与先进等离子体技术研发
俄罗斯国家研究中心“库尔恰托夫研究所”(National Research Centre "Kurchatov Institute")将在2027至2029年期间，从俄罗斯联邦财政预算中获得约57亿卢布(Rubles)的专项资金支持。该笔财政拨款将专门用于推进受控热核聚变(Controlled Thermonuclear Fusion)关键技术攻坚，以及创新型等离子体技术(Plasma Technologies)的研发与试验验证。
上述资金规划明确载于俄罗斯国家杜马(State Duma)电子数据库公示的2027—2029年度联邦预算法案草案说明文件中。按照拟定的三年预算编制周期，该专项研发计划将分年度有序划拨：2027年拟投入近19.5亿卢布，2028年计划注资18.7亿卢布，2029年继续下达18.7亿卢布支持科研攻关。
作为俄罗斯核科学与能源技术的核心策源地，库尔恰托夫研究所承担着聚变堆磁约束、耐辐照结构材料研发以及特种等离子体源设计的重任。受控热核聚变技术被全球科学界公认为有望彻底解决人类终极能源需求的战略方向，而高能等离子体物理与控制技术在微电子芯片制造、高端材料表面改性、放射性医疗及综合能源系统中亦具备广泛的跨界应用价值。
随着全球对下一代清洁基荷能源竞争的加剧，该项为期三年的连续财政注资，将进一步巩固俄罗斯在托卡马克装置运行、等离子体约束加热等尖端物理工程领域的自主研发能力，并深度赋能相关国家大科学工程与跨国热核研究项目的履约推进。

俄罗斯原子能公司向亚美尼亚提议新建VVER-1000核电机组
俄罗斯国家原子能集团(Rosatom)总经理阿列克谢·利哈乔夫近日在埃里温表示，该公司已向亚美尼亚政府提出建设千兆瓦级VVER-1000核电机组的具体建议。该建议基于对亚美尼亚至2040年电力需求的评估，拟采用俄成熟压水堆技术VVER-1000，其具备3+代安全系统与经济电价优势，且已在俄罗斯、印度、伊朗等国建成投产。俄方称此方案为国际市场最优选择，并愿将项目打造为吸引国际供应商的综合合作项目。
此前，利哈乔夫与亚美尼亚总理尼科尔·帕希尼扬及副总理会谈，重点讨论亚美尼亚核电站延寿至2036年问题。俄方通报，延寿项目第一阶段已完成，获准继续运行。目前，俄方与亚美尼亚核电封闭股份公司签署的框架合同正推进安全系统现代化，确保2026至2036年可靠供电。现有亚美尼亚核电站位于梅察莫尔市，装有两台VVER-440机组，首台于1976年投运，第二台在1995年重启，2021年经俄协助完成改造。
俄驻亚美尼亚大使谢尔盖·科佩尔金参与会谈。俄原子能公司表示，将提供全系列核电技术，包括大、中、小功率机组，但当前优先推进VVER-1000方案。未来几个月，亚美尼亚将比较不同供应商方案以作出选择。

亚马逊签署长期购电协议支撑30亿美元投资：卡尔弗特克利夫斯核电站拟实施190兆瓦功率提升并申请延寿
美国联合能源公司(Constellation Energy)与科技巨头亚马逊(Amazon)于9月30日正式宣布达成一项长期购电协议(Power Purchase Agreement, PPA)。该协议将全面支撑针对马里兰州卡尔弗特克利夫斯核电站(Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant)超过30亿美元的重大基础设施升级投资，其中核心规划包括为两台现役压水堆(Pressurized Water Reactor, PWR)机组实施总计190兆瓦的功率提升。
这项为期20年的购电协议锁定了690兆瓦的电力供应配额，其中涵盖了新增的扩增容量。该项长期商业承购承诺不仅为总装机容量达1.79吉瓦的核电基地注入了稳定的资金回报预期，更为联合能源公司启动后续长达20年的机组二次延寿(Subsequent License Renewal, SLR)申请提供了坚实的经济支撑。新增的190兆瓦发电量计划于2030年至2032年期间分阶段实现并网发电。
虽然联合能源公司尚未公布具体的工程承包商名单及30亿美元资金在功率提升、全厂现代化改造与延寿工程间的具体切分比例，但前期的硬件技术改造早已拉开序幕。早在2025年2月，联合能源即宣布投资约1亿美元用于关键电气系统与主设备的翻新，包括泵类、电机、特种阀门、控制棒驱动机构(Control Rod Drive Mechanism, CRDM)的翻修与更换，以及13千伏主变压器的深度大修;后续还投入6800万美元升级了厂区变电站的24台高压断路器。
在核安全审评方面，美国核管理委员会(Nuclear Regulatory Commission, NRC)已于10月1日与联合能源公司举行闭门会议，深入对接卡尔弗特克利夫斯1号和2号机组后续的许可证修订申请(License Amendment Request, LAR)。NRC高级公共事务官斯科特·伯内尔(Scott Burnell)指出，业主方须按法定程序公开提交功率提升或延寿申请文件，监管机构在确认受理立案后方可确立具体的审评时间表。
卡尔弗特克利夫斯核电站在全美核电史上拥有多项技术标杆意义：两台由燃烧工程公司供货的反应堆不仅在1977年成为全美首例获批拉伸功率提升的机组，还在2000年成为全美首座获得首次延寿许可的商业核电站。目前，1号机组与2号机组的现行运行许可证将分别于2034年7月31日和2036年8月13日到期。
在2026年完成的1号机组大修换料窗口期内，联合能源耗资近9000万美元推进了重型装备更替，其中包括成功吊装一台价值480万美元、重达151吨的大型变压器。通过与科技企业签署长期清洁电力长协，卡尔弗特克利夫斯核电站正构建起“算力用能支撑深层核能技改、核能扩容保障零碳电网”的全新商业闭环模式。

title: 科学网-研究显示简单脑力活动有助改善老年人认知障碍

研究显示简单脑力活动有助改善老年人认知障碍
英国南安普敦大学日前发布消息说，一项大规模研究显示，拼图、学习新技能、参加社交活动等简单的脑力活动，配合运动和健康饮食建议，有助改善老年人的认知障碍。
研究人员对超过1.15万名60岁至85岁、存在不同程度认知障碍的人进行了为期12个月的研究。参与者被分成三组：第一组参与者获得了研究人员提供的有针对性的简要建议，包括通过体育锻炼、健康饮食和脑力刺激活动来维持认知健康；第二组还可使用提供脑力训练和相关建议的网站；第三组则额外获得护士等工作人员通过面谈、电话或电子邮件提供的简短咨询。
结果显示，12个月后，三组中不再检测出认知障碍的人数比例分别约为28%、33%和32%。研究人员说，脑力刺激活动包括拼拼图、玩脑力训练游戏、演奏乐器、参加合唱团、学习新语言以及参与社交活动等。由于多数参与者原本已经具有较健康的运动和饮食习惯，研究人员认为，认知功能改善可能主要与这些脑力活动有关。
相关研究已发表于期刊《柳叶刀·初级保健》。

title: 科学网-OpenAI安全系统团队负责人辞职
content:
OpenAI安全系统团队负责人辞职
当地时间10月3日，据美国方面消息，OpenAI安全系统团队负责人大卫·罗宾逊已辞职。
OpenAI一名发言人表示，罗宾逊于上周离开公司，此前还曾负责公司的政策规划工作，并参与人工智能安全透明度工作，包括开发和发布模型“系统卡”。
罗宾逊在《大西洋月刊》发表文章称，他认为目前人工智能企业的发展方式“不可接受”，问题不仅在于具体安全规则和法律，还在于企业文化。他表示，OpenAI长期采用通过发现问题、再不断改进安全防护措施的“迭代部署”方式，但随着人工智能系统能力不断增强，这种做法可能导致安全失误的影响越来越大。
罗宾逊还提到，OpenAI此前曾发生人工智能代理意外运行以及模型绕过互联网访问限制等安全事件，并认为相关问题与行业快速开发和频繁试错的工作方式有关。此前，OpenAI称因“处理敏感材料，而非举报安全问题”，解雇了三名安全研究人员。
此前，澳大利亚总理阿尔巴尼斯在纽约出席第81届联合国大会期间透露，OpenAI的一个智能体今年6月曾侵入澳大利亚政府网站。该AI智能体不仅访问了公开文件，还访问了非公开文件。9月28日，OpenAI公开致歉，承认事件处置存在不当，并承诺承担责任，称要“重建澳大利亚民众的信任”。
当地时间10月2日，美国开放人工智能研究中心（OpenAI）披露，有第二家澳大利亚政府机构遭到了入侵。OpenAI在一份声明中表示，一个人工智能模型获取了新南威尔士州某政府机构保存的火灾统计数据，而这些数据并未由该部门向公众公开。OpenAI称，公司是在针对“模型行为偏离预期”展开的更大范围调查过程中发现了这一事件。（总台记者 张颖哲）

title: 科学网-《自然》（20261001出版）一周论文导读
content:
《自然》（20261001出版）一周论文导读
Nature,1 October 2026, Volume 658, Issue 8134
《自然》，2026年10月1日，第658卷，8134期
材料科学Materials Science
Anomalous metal and superconducting phases in rhombohedral graphene
菱方石墨烯中的反常金属相与超导相
▲ 作者：Anna Okounkova, Abigail Sohm, Tobias Faehndrich, Manish Kumar, Derek Waleffe, Jiaqiang Yan, et al.
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11033-1
二维超导现已在石墨烯基体系中得到充分证实，诸多相关体系均观测到非传统配对的证据。然而，在本应呈现显著超导特征的若干栅控相中，电阻并不会随降温而消失，而是饱和于某一有限数值。
研究组对二硒化钨（WSe
）基底上菱方石墨烯中的这种行为开展了系统研究，发现在栅压空间内，既有零电阻超导区域，也有电阻有限饱和的区域。零磁场下，这些区域在栅压空间中呈现为孤立“口袋”；除此之外，它们表现出高度相似的现象学，包括当温度、垂直磁场与电流超过临界值时，会突变为正常态。
施加微弱面内磁场可使这些口袋扩大并相互合并，而不会定性改变其行为；在毫开级基温下，零电阻态与有限电阻态之间形成清晰的分界。该有限电阻态复现了反常金属的关键现象学。异常金属态在超导薄膜中已被观测数十年，但尚无公认的理论解释。
超高纯度菱方石墨烯具备可调性与可重复性，严格约束了各类外源性机制解释，也为理解该物理行为提供了一个全新研究平台。
▲ Abstract：
Two-dimensional superconductivity is now well established in graphene-based systems, with many such realizations showing evidence for unconventional pairing. Yet, in several of the gate-tuned phases that otherwise exhibit clear signatures of superconductivity, the resistance does not vanish as temperature is lowered, instead saturating at a finite value. Here we report a systematic study of this behaviour in rhombohedral graphene on a WSe
substrate, finding regions of gate space with zero-resistance superconductivity alongside others with finite saturation resistance. At zero magnetic field, these regions appear as isolated pockets in gate space that otherwise exhibit very similar phenomenology, including abrupt transitions to the normal state as temperature, perpendicular magnetic field and current are raised above critical values. A small in-plane field expands and merges these pockets without qualitatively altering their behaviour, producing a sharp boundary at millikelvin base temperature between states of zero or finite resistance. The finite-resistance state reproduces key phenomenology associated with the anomalous metal, a state that has been observed in thin-film superconductors for decades but lacks an accepted theoretical explanation. The tunability and reproducibility of ultra-clean rhombohedral graphene place strong constraints on extrinsic explanations and provide a new platform for understanding this behaviour.
Stacking-induced direct band gap in CVD-grown 1H MoS
bilayers
化学气相沉积制备1H MoS
双层中堆叠效应诱导的直接带隙
▲ 作者：Tilo H. Yang, I-Tong Chen, Min-Jia Zhang, Ju-Yi Huang, Tzu-Hao Kuo, Shao-Yu Chen, et al.
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11069-3
双层过渡金属二硫化物相比其单层体系具备更优异的电子特性，例如更高的载流子迁移率与可电切换的极性，使其成为下一代晶体管与滑动铁电器件颇具吸引力的候选材料。然而，其固有的间接带隙严重限制了光发射，阻碍了这类材料在光电子系统中的集成。
研究组报道了通过两步化学气相沉积工艺制备得到具有1H堆叠结构的双层二硫化钼（MoS
），实现原子级精准的纵向排布。角分辨光电子能谱与密度泛函理论计算证实，该1H型双层材料具有直接带隙。光致发光测试结果显示，该材料激子发射增强，且无间接带隙特征。
此外，在共振与非共振激发条件下，这类双层结构的谷极化强度均高于单层，主要源于顶层材料中谷间散射受到抑制。综上，该研究证明1H MoS
可作为堆叠工程量子材料的模型体系，并凸显其在谷电子学与光电子学领域中的应用潜力。
▲ Abstract：
Bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides offer superior electronic properties over their monolayer counterparts, such as higher carrier mobility and electrically switchable polarity, positioning them as attractive candidates for next-generation transistors and sliding ferroelectric devices. However, their inherent indirect band gap severely limits light emission, hindering their integration into optoelectronic systems. Here we show bilayer MoS
with 1H stacking obtained by a two-step chemical vapour deposition process, yielding atomically precise vertical alignment. The 1H bilayers exhibit a direct band gap, as confirmed by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations. Photoluminescence measurements show intensified excitonic emission and the absence of indirect bandgap features. Furthermore, these bilayers exhibit stronger valley polarization than monolayers under both resonant and nonresonant excitation, primarily because of the suppressed intervalley scattering in the top layer. Together, these results establish 1H MoS
as a model system for stacking-engineered quantum materials and underscore its potential for valleytronic and optoelectronic applications.
信息科学Information Science
Scalable decision-making for games of imperfect information
不完备信息博弈的可扩展决策
▲ 作者：Samuel Sokota, Eugene Vinitsky, Hengyuan Hu, Zhiyuan Fan, J. Zico Kolter & Gabriele Farina
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11036-y
现实场景下的决策通常包含隐藏信息，即某一智能体未知、但另一智能体掌握的信息。遗憾的是，大量隐藏信息的存在，会使得现有强化学习与搜索方法失效。
尽管产业界投入了数百万美元开展研究，但在《西洋陆军棋》这款具备大规模隐藏信息的桌面兵棋中，人工智能（AI）始终无法达到人类顶尖选手水平。
研究组提出Ataraxos，一款用于西洋陆军棋的AI。该模型基于其自研的通用算法，可支持隐藏信息场景下的自对弈强化学习以及测试阶段搜索。Ataraxos以较大优势击败了史上战绩最辉煌的西洋陆军棋人类玩家；据研究组所知，这是该游戏史上首个超越人类水平的AI成绩，且相比以往工作，算力与数据消耗降低多个数量级。
借助同一套技术，研究组还构建了超越人类水平的速攻版西洋陆军棋AI，以及用于《花火》、《斗地主》的顶尖AI，均具备低成本与高样本效率。该方法在对抗类、合作类与团队类博弈任务中均取得成功，为大量隐藏信息条件下的强化学习与搜索提供了一套设计范式，而这正是战略决策领域长期追求的目标。
▲ Abstract：
Real-world decision-making generally involves hidden information, that is, information that is unknown to one agent but possessed by another. Unfortunately, the presence of large amounts of hidden information renders established reinforcement learning and search approaches ineffective. Even with multimillion-dollar industrial research efforts, top-human-level play at Stratego—a board wargame with hidden information on a massive scale—has remained beyond the reach of artificial intelligence (AI). Here we introduce Ataraxos, an AI for Stratego based on general techniques that we developed for both self-play reinforcement learning and test-time search under hidden information. Ataraxos defeated the most decorated human Stratego player of all time by a large margin—achieving, to our knowledge, the first superhuman result in the game’s history—while consuming orders of magnitude less compute and data than previous efforts. Using the same techniques, we built a superhuman AI for Barrage Stratego and state-of-the-art AIs for Hanabi and dou dizhu, all with low cost and high sample efficiency. The success of this approach across adversarial, cooperative and team games establishes a design pattern for reinforcement learning and search that is effective under large amounts of hidden information, a longstanding desideratum of the field of strategic decision-making.
化学Chemistry
Programmable remodelling of carbon–nitrogen connectivity in amines
胺类化合物中C–N连接的可编程重塑
▲ 作者：James D. Robinson, Fran
ois Richard, Kohl A. Ratkovich, Joseph M. Phelps & Matthew J. Gaunt
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11009-1
叔胺是生物活性分子中普遍存在的结构基元，在分子识别与分子功能中发挥核心作用。其中，叔苄胺在发现化学中尤为重要，其易于由丰富的构建模块组装而成，可作为先导化合物生成的起点，兼具良好的理化性质与结合特性。
尽管这类化合物易于合成，但因其核心C–N连接方式基本固定，只能对苄胺衍生物进行多样化，无法直接获得结构迥异的芳基-烷基胺骨架。要想突破这一局限，需要在已充分构建的胺骨架上直接且选择性地重构C–N连接方式。
研究组表明，借助C–N的催化重塑，叔苄胺可由静态骨架转变为可编程分子多样化平台。叔苄胺与双官能亲电试剂发生N-烷基化反应，生成季铵盐中间体，可在钯催化下发生C–N的裂解与重构。
这一概念首先通过叔苄胺的一碳同系物得到验证，更重要的是，其建立了一套通用策略，能够在已充分构建胺骨架的C–N之间，程序化插入各类模块化单元，从单个碳原子到包括烃链、杂环和芳基的复杂分子片段不等。该技术为胺类骨架的可编程多样化开辟了路径，助力系统探索胺分子的键连方式与分子骨架结构。
▲ Abstract：
Tertiary amines are ubiquitous motifs in biologically active molecules, in which they play central parts in molecular recognition and function. Among these, tertiary benzylamines are particularly prominent in discovery chemistry as readily assembled starting points for lead generation from abundant building blocks, with favourable physicochemical and binding properties. However, despite their accessibility, the core C–N connectivity of these frameworks remains effectively locked, confining diversification to benzylamine derivatives and preventing direct access to structurally distinct aryl–alkylamine architectures. Overcoming this limitation requires direct and selective reconfiguration of C–N connectivity within fully elaborated amine scaffolds. Here we show that tertiary benzylamines can be transformed from static scaffolds into programmable platforms for molecular diversification through catalytic remodelling of their C–N bonds. N-alkylation with a bifunctional electrophile generates a quaternary ammonium intermediate that encodes palladium-catalysed disassembly and reconfiguration of C–N connectivity. This concept is first exemplified through one-carbon homologation of tertiary benzylamines and, more significantly, establishes a general strategy for programmable insertion of modular units—ranging from single carbon atoms to complex molecular fragments, including hydrocarbon chains, heterocycles and aryl groups—directly across the C–N bond on fully elaborated amine scaffolds. This ability opens a route to programmable diversification of amine frameworks, enabling systematic exploration of amine connectivity and molecular architecture.
地球科学Earth Science
Agricultural liming is a carbon sink in the Mississippi River Basin
农业施用石灰是密西西比河流域的碳汇
▲ 作者：Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, Christopher T. Reinhard, Yoshiki Kanzaki, Samuel Shou-En Tsao, Beck Woollen, Tom Reershemius, et al.
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11040-2
向耕地施用碳酸盐矿物，即农业石灰改良，是一项用于缓解土壤酸化的传统措施。尽管石灰改良能够提升作物产量，但该过程也被视作农业二氧化碳（CO
研究组利用密西西比河流域长达百年尺度的农业石灰施用记录与人为酸输入数据开展研究，结果表明在过去一个世纪中，农业石灰改良起到了净碳汇作用。
河流碱度通量记录显示，1900年以来施加的农用石灰约90%的理论固碳潜力（约0.44 GtCO
）已在流域尺度上实现；受土壤阳离子交换与溶质输运过程影响，该固碳效应存在十年尺度的时间滞后。
上述结果与土壤阳离子通量的反应性输运模拟结果一致，模型表明：在中和土壤酸性库产生初期排放脉冲之后，体系才会出现净二氧化碳移除效应。现行核算框架隐含采用不完备的反事实情景，将二氧化碳排放归因于石灰施用本身，而非驱动二氧化碳释放的人为酸输入。
若以存在人为酸输入作为反事实基准进行评估，在数十年至百年时间尺度上，密西西比河流域的农业石灰改良表现为净碳汇。该结果表明，优化土壤pH调控可在降低农业温室气体排放的同时，提升作物产量、改善土壤健康。

Application of carbonate minerals to arable lands, known as agricultural liming, is a long-standing practice for counteracting soil acidification. Although liming boosts crop yields, it is also considered a source of agricultural carbon dioxide (CO

Here we show, using century-scale records of agricultural liming and anthropogenic acidity inputs for the Mississippi River Basin, that agricultural liming has acted as a net carbon sink over the past century. Records of river alkalinity fluxes suggest that approximately 90% of the ideal CO

These results are consistent with reactive transport modelling of soil cation throughput, which indicates that net CO removal potential of agricultural lime added since 1900 (approximately 0.44 GtCO
